PART-II 
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Recommendation No. 1 
Need for Proper and Realistic Budgetary Planning 
 
The Committee note that while the Total Central Government Outlay 
has increased steadily from ₹39,44,909 crore in 2022-23 to ₹53,47,315 crore 
in 2026-27, the share of the Ministry has not grown proportionately. The 
Ministry’s share, which stood at 1.94% in 2022-23 and 1.91% in 2025-26, has 
declined to 1.60% in 2026-27 which is the lowest in the five-year period. 
Further, against the projected outlay of ₹97,644.51 crore for 2026-27, the 
approved Budget Estimate is ₹85,522.39 crore, reflecting a reduction of 
₹12,122.12 crore (12.41%). The Committee also note that such reductions 
between projected outlay and approved Budget Estimates have been 
persistent over the years i.e. 22.82% in 2022-23, 11.52% in 2023-24 and 
17.25% in 2024-25, with the only exception being the year 2025-26.  
 
The Committee also note that despite increasing urbanisation and 
rising demand for housing, water supply, sanitation and urban transport, 
the Ministry’s relative share in the Central Budget has declined and its 
projections are routinely curtailed at the approval stage except in FY 2025-
26. The Committee feel that such persistent gaps between projected outlay 
and Budgetary allocation are linked to the actual utilisation trends, 
highlighting a systemic mismatch between projection and implementation 
capacity. With the need to address the issues of such stark gaps between 
the Ministry’s budgetary projections and actual utilisation, the Committee 
recommend the Ministry : 
(i) to adopt a more realistic and evidence-based forecasting mechanism 
aligned with actual implementation capacity at the State level;  
(ii) to formulate and present a clear and time-bound roadmap for 
progressively enhancing Ministry’s share in the Total Central Outlay, 

79 
 
commensurate with the expanding urban infrastructure needs and 
services, delivery obligations aligned with the vision of ‘Viksit 
Bharat’ in 2047; and 
(iii) to institute robust expenditure monitoring and mid-year review 
mechanisms to ensure timely utilization of allocated funds under key 
schemes and other urban infrastructure programmes, enabling 
corrective action within the same FY to prevent persistent 
underutilization. 
 
Recommendation No. 2 
Need for Timely Utilisation of Funds  
 
The Committee note that the gap between Budget Estimates (BE), 
Revised Estimates (RE) and Actual Expenditure (AE) of the Ministry has 
widened significantly in recent years. While utilisation remained close to 
RE in 2022-23 and 2023-24, the position deteriorated in 2024-25 and 2025-
26. In 2025-26, the BE of ₹96,777 crore was sharply reduced at RE stage to 
₹57,203.78 crore (a reduction of nearly 40%). The actual expenditure as on 
20.02.2026 stands at ₹40,967.62 crore, which is only 71.62% of RE implying 
that nearly 28.38% of the revised allocation is to be spent in the last 39 
days of the financial year. Scheme-wise analysis shows uneven 
performance. While AMRUT and PMAY (Urban) show utilisation above 79–
80% of RE, schemes such as PM-eBus Sewa (17.87%), CITIIS 2.0 (0.37%), 
PM SVANidhi (60.99%), DJAY (45.60%) and PHE (40.29%) show slow 
progress. Further, unspent balances under various schemes amount to 
₹5,806.27 crore, with substantial balances under Smart Cities Mission 
(₹2,012.64 crore), SBM (₹1,238.90 crore) and AMRUT (₹1,213.01 crore). The 
amount surrendered has also risen sharply from ₹1,157.31 crore in 2022-23 
to ₹32,291.34 crore in 2024-25 indicating serious issues in expenditure 
planning and utilisation. 
The Committee take note of the Ministry’s submission that 
expenditure depends substantially on the spending capacity of States 
under the SNA-SPARSH mechanism, which requires States to incur 

80 
 
expenditure before the Central share is released. The Ministry has also 
cited delays in approval of major schemes such as the National Urban 
Digital Mission (NUDM), Urban Challenge Fund and the Scheme for 
Industrial Housing, involving an outlay of ₹13,750 crore, as factors 
affecting utilisation. While these constraints are acknowledged, the 
Committee are of the considered view that repeated large-scale reductions 
at the RE stage, uneven scheme performance and growing unspent 
balances point to deeper issues in budgeting realism, inter-governmental 
coordination and monitoring. The Committee, therefore, recommend that 
the Ministry: 
(i) to undertake a thorough review of Budgeting exercise so as to better 
align Budgetary Estimate, Revised Estimate and Actual Expenditure;  
(ii) to address procedural bottlenecks under fund flow mechanisms 
such as SNA-SPARSH;  
(iii) to fix scheme-wise spending targets at regular intervals, ideally 
every quarter, and review them closely to ensure timely use of funds; 
(iv) to strengthen institutional capacity of States and Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs) for improved fund absorption; and  
(v) to ensure that expenditure is evenly paced throughout the year 
avoiding year-end concentration, so as to uphold both fiscal 
prudence and implementation quality. 
 
Recommendation No. 3 
Strengthening Implementation and Financial Discipline under PMAY 
(Urban) 
 
The Committee note that while Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana–Urban 
(PMAY-U) has achieved significant scale in terms of sanctions (122.22 lakh 
houses) and grounding (114.59 lakh houses), actual completion stands at 
96.65 lakh houses, indicating that a sizeable number of houses are still 
pending completion. The Committee further observe that Budget Estimates 
for 2025–26 was drastically reduced at the Revised Estimate stage from 
₹23,294 crore to ₹7,800 crore, and actual expenditure as on 05.01.2026 is 

81 
 
only ₹3,874.84 crore, reflecting slow fund utilisation. Although the Ministry 
has attributed this to low utilisation of “Mother Sanctions” by States and 
the initial phase of PMAY-U 2.0, the Committee are of the view that such 
sharp reductions and modest actual spending point towards underlying 
weaknesses in expenditure planning and implementation pace. 
The State-wise data also reveal uneven physical and financial 
progress. Large States such as Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra 
Pradesh, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh account for a major 
share of completions; however, noticeable gaps between sanctioned and 
completed houses persist in Telangana, Bihar, Jharkhand, Rajasthan and 
Haryana. In the North Eastern region, Manipur, Meghalaya and Arunachal 
Pradesh show comparatively low completion levels. On the financial side, 
while around 85–86% of sanctioned central assistance has been released 
nationally, gaps remain in States such as Telangana, Bihar, Odisha and 
Punjab. In States like Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Rajasthan and 
West Bengal, substantial central assistance has already been released but 
completion of houses is yet to fully catch up, indicating delays in 
converting financial support into completed dwelling units. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry that: 
(i) Budget Estimates under the scheme be projected more realistically 
so as to avoid sharp reductions at the Revised Estimate stage and 
low actual expenditure at the end of the financial year; 
(ii) a strengthened review and coordination mechanism be put in place 
with periodic progress assessment to ensure that central assistance 
is translated into completed dwelling units within the stipulated 
timeframe; and 
(iii) the adequacy of existing central financial assistance per dwelling 
unit be reviewed and suitably enhanced, wherever necessary, 
keeping in view rising construction costs, so that beneficiaries are 
not burdened and projects are completed in a timely and sustainable 
manner. 
 
 

82 
 
Recommendation No. 4 
Slow progress of Light House Projects (LHP) under PMAY(U) 
 
The Committee note that under PMAY-U 1.0 six Light House Projects 
(LHPs), each comprising over 1,000 houses with allied infrastructure 
facilities are being constructed at Indore (Madhya Pradesh), Rajkot 
(Gujarat), Chennai (Tamil Nadu), Ranchi (Jharkhand), Agartala (Tripura) and 
Lucknow (Uttar Pradesh). The foundation stones for six LHPs were laid by 
Hon’ble Prime Minister on January 1, 2021. The Committee also note that 
these houses have been constructed using six different innovative 
technologies identified through the Global Housing Technological 
Challenge-India (GHTC-India). It has also been submitted by the Ministry 
that these LHPs will serve as live laboratories for all stakeholders 
facilitating dissemination of knowledge about these technologies in terms 
of cost and time effectiveness, resilience, environmental friendliness, 
faster construction etc. and promoting their adoption in house 
construction activities. Further, the Hon’ble Prime Minister has inaugurated 
LHP Chennai on 26th May 2022, LHP Rajkot on 19th October 2022, LHP 
Indore on 5th October 2023 and LHP Lucknow & LHP Ranchi on 10th March 
2024. The LHP Agartala is in advanced stage of construction. 
The Committee in their Seventeenth Report (2022-23) on “Evaluation 
of Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban)” had 
recommended for speedy completion of LHPs and for additional central 
assistance for LHP projects, Agartala, Tripura. The Committee are pleased 
to learn through the Action Taken replies furnished by the Government on 
Committee’s recommendation that a conscious decision has been taken by 
the Ministry to enhance the Technology Innovation Grants (TIG) share so 
that the burden on EWS beneficiaries can be substantially reduced and 
LHP projects are implemented successfully. The TIG has been revised from 
₹2.00 lakh per Dwelling Unit (DU) or 20% of the estimated cost per DU, 
whichever is less to ₹4.00 lakh per DU or, 40% of the tendered cost per DU, 
whichever is less in case of LHP Chennai (Tamil Nadu), Ranchi 
(Jharkhand), Indore (Madhya Pradesh), Rajkot (Gujarat) and Lucknow (Uttar 

83 
 
Pradesh). For LHP Agartala (Tripura), TIG has been increased to ₹5.00 lakh 
per DU or, 40% of the tendered cost per DU, whichever is less, which is 
already higher as compared to other LHP States. The TIG is in addition to 
the existing funding of ₹1.5 lakh per DU under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana 
- Urban (PMAY-U). The Committee are of the view that the additional central 
assistance was provided to LHP Agartala for timely completion of the 
project and any further delay in completion of the Agartala Light House 
Project would defeat the very purpose and objective of the initiative. The 
Committee therefore, recommend that the Ministry review the project’s 
progress on regular basis, provide necessary handholding to the State of 
Tripura for speedy completion of the Dwelling Units and furnish a status 
report to the Committee at the earliest. 
 
Recommendation No. 5 
Ensuring Wider and Balanced Implementation of ARHC across States 
 
Affordable Rental Housing Complex (ARHC) scheme was introduced 
as a sub-scheme of PMAY (U) in July, 2020 and since September, 2024 is 
being implemented as a vertical under PMAY(U) 2.0 through two models i.e. 
Model-I, which envisages conversion of existing government-funded 
vacant houses into rental housing through PPP or public agencies for 25 
years; and Model-II, which provides for construction, operation and 
maintenance of new rental housing units by public or private entities on 
their own land for 25 years. However, progress under both the models has 
been uneven. Under Model-I, against 83,534 vacant houses identified, only 
5,783 units have been converted into ARHCs, while 7,413 units are under 
process, leaving a very large stock of vacant houses unutilised. States/UTs 
such as Delhi and Maharashtra, despite having 29,112 and 32,345 vacant 
houses respectively, have reported no conversion under the scheme. The 
Committee further note that out of 5,783 houses converted under Model-I in 
eight cities, 4,605 units have been occupied by beneficiaries so far, while 
1,178 units remain vacant. Under Model-II, although 83,298 units have been 
approved nationwide, only 36,450 units have been completed and occupied 

84 
 
so far, with the overwhelming share concentrated at Sriperumbudur, Hosur 
and Chennai in Tamil Nadu. Many approved projects in other States remain 
at early stages of completion. This indicates slow progress, limited 
geographical spread and inadequate reporting on actual utilisation of 
assets created. 
The Committee are of the view that the objectives of ARHC, which 
aims to provide dignified, affordable rental housing to urban migrants, poor 
and other vulnerable groups close to their workplaces, cannot be fully 
realised unless vacant houses are swiftly converted and newly approved 
units are completed and occupied in a time-bound manner. The Committee, 
therefore, recommend to the Ministry:  
(i) to prepare a time-bound State/UT-wise action plan for conversion of 
vacant houses under Model-I, particularly in States/UTs with large 
inventories such as Delhi and Maharashtra and actively resolve 
administrative or coordination issues hindering implementation; 
(ii) to establish a system to oversee and ensure that the houses lying 
vacant in various States/UTs which are being considered under 
Model-I of AHRC are first appropriately retrofitted, repaired and 
upgraded, wherever necessary, to make them habitable; 
(iii) to set strict timelines for completion and operationalisation of 
approved units under Model-II, with periodic review of construction 
and occupancy status; 
(iv) to strengthen monitoring and coordination with States/UTs and 
private partners so that both conversion of existing vacant houses 
and construction of new rental units translate into functional, fully 
occupied housing complexes serving the intended beneficiaries; and 
(v) to undertake a comprehensive national assessment of demand for 
affordable rental housing for urban migrants and to fix clear 
State/UT-wise targets for the number of ARHC dwelling units. 
 
 
 
 

85 
 
Recommendation No. 6 
Need for affordable Rent Fixation and Operationalisation of Incentives 
under ARHC 
 
The Committee note that under the Affordable Rental Housing 
Complexes (ARHC) scheme, Dwelling Units may consist of Single/Double 
Bedroom units (30/60 sqm) and Dormitory beds (10 sqm), with basic 
facilities such as kitchen, toilet and bathroom as prescribed in the 
operational guidelines. Further, as per the guidelines, rent under Model–I 
which permits conversion of existing government-funded vacant houses, is 
to be fixed by the local authority based on a local survey conducted prior 
to issuance of the Request for Proposal (RFP). Under Model–II which 
allows construction, operation and maintenance by public/private entities, 
the initial affordable rent is to be fixed by the concerned entity based on a 
local survey. Rent is permitted to be enhanced biennially by 8%, subject to 
a maximum cumulative increase of 20% over five years. 
The guidelines further provide for various fiscal and non-fiscal 
incentives to improve project viability and ensure affordability. These 
include concessional project finance, Income Tax and GST exemptions, 
Technology Innovation Grant (TIG), additional FAR/FSI up to 50% free of 
cost, land-use relaxations, single-window approvals, levy of municipal 
charges at par with residential properties and provision of trunk 
infrastructure up to the project site by States/UTs without additional cost. 
The Committee observe that rent fixation is entirely decentralised 
and the Ministry does not prescribe uniform rent rates nor maintain 
centralized data regarding rent levels across cities. Similarly, 
implementation of incentives such as additional FAR/FSI, land-use 
permissions, municipal charge parity and trunk infrastructure provision 
varies across States/UTs depending upon local regulations and policy 
notifications. With regard to fiscal incentives, including Income Tax and 
GST exemptions, the Committee are apprised that the Ministry does not 
directly administer these benefits project-wise and has indicated that the 
matter is being taken up with the concerned authorities. 

86 
 
The Committee are of the view that while flexibility to States/UTs is 
necessary given that land and housing are State subjects, the core intent of 
the Scheme to provide “affordable” rental housing to the urban migrants 
must not get sidelined. The Committee are also of the view that the 
absence of a broad guiding framework and centralized monitoring of rents 
may lead to variations that affect affordability for migrant workers. The 
Committee further observe that uneven implementation of incentives such 
as additional FAR/FSI, trunk infrastructure, tax exemptions and municipal 
charge parity may adversely impact project viability and could ultimately 
result in higher rents. 
In view of the above, the Committee recommend the Ministry : 
(i) to assess feasibility of issuing indicative rent benchmarks to ensure 
‘affordability’ for urban migrants while retaining flexibility for local 
conditions and to develop a centralized system to capture State-wise 
data on rent fixation, revisions, occupancy levels and incentives 
availed under both models of ARHC; 
(ii) to ensure that ARHC projects are prioritised in locations near major 
employment hubs and industrial areas to ensure higher occupancy 
and reduced commuting burden on beneficiaries; 
(iii) to direct States/UTs to strictly implement provisions relating to free 
additional FAR/FSI, land-use relaxations, residential-rate municipal 
charges and timely provision of trunk infrastructure as mandated in 
the operational guidelines; and 
(iv) to actively pursue operationalisation of Income Tax and GST 
exemptions and ensure that such fiscal benefits translate into 
affordable rents for tenants. 
 
Recommendation No. 7 
Strengthening Financial Planning, Monitoring and Timely Completion under 
AMRUT 2.0 
 
The Committee note that although the Budget Estimates for AMRUT 
2.0 were kept at ₹8,000 crore in 2023-24 and 2024-25 and enhanced to 

87 
 
₹10,000 crore in 2025–26, the Revised Estimates were scaled down in 
successive years due to slow pace of expenditure. In 2025–26, only 
₹5,569.21 crore or 74.25% of RE had been utilised as of January 2026. The 
Ministry has primarily attributed this to delays in onboarding States onto 
the SNA SPARSH platform. The Committee are of the view that recurring 
reductions at the RE stage reflect overestimation at the BE stage and 
weaknesses in expenditure planning and absorption capacity. 
The Committee further note that against the total approved Central 
share of ₹76,760 crore, only ₹18,757.16 crore has been released so far, 
which is significantly lower than the total approved outlay, and out of this, 
₹15,161.94 crore has been utilised, reflecting an overall financial progress 
of 80.83% against the funds released. While the overall physical grounding 
of projects stands at 78.65%, the inter-State variations remain significant. 
Several States have demonstrated commendable performance in both 
physical and financial progress. However, a number of States are lagging in 
physical achievement, while few show low financial utilisation.  
The Committee are of the considered view that with AMRUT 2.0 
entering its final phase, delays in grounding projects and uneven utilisation 
of funds could hinder timely completion and the fulfilment of its key 
objectives, especially universal water supply and sewerage coverage. The 
Committee accordingly stress that timely completion of ongoing projects, 
efficient utilisation of allocated funds and reduction of inter-State 
disparities are essential to ensuring durable and sustainable urban 
infrastructure outcomes under the Mission.  
The Committee therefore recommend that to achieve the physical 
and financial target set under the Mission, the Ministry must focus on 
handholding of lagging States so as to accelerate physical grounding and 
completion of remaining projects and ensure that mission objectives are 
met within stipulated timelines. 
 
 
 

88 
 
Recommendation No. 8 
Need for Adequate Financial Allocation and Expedited Remediation of 
Legacy Dumpsites under Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 
 
The Committee note that under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 
2.0, notable progress has been reported in door-to-door collection (96.54% 
wards), source segregation (88.08% wards) and waste processing (81.65% 
of total waste generated). Further, 1,193 cities have been certified as 
Garbage Free Cities (GFC) with varying star ratings. However, the 
Committee observe certain critical concerns regarding financial 
management and remediation of legacy dumpsites. 
On the financial front, there is a consistent gap between the 
Ministry’s projected requirements, Budget Estimates (BE), Revised 
Estimates (RE) and actual expenditure. In the last four years, allocations at 
the BE stage were lower than projections and were further reduced at the 
RE stage. While expenditure remained close to RE in earlier years, in 2025–
26 only ₹1,321.15 crore has been spent as on 17.02.2026 against an RE of 
₹2,000 crore which is about 66%. Further, for 2026-27, against a projected 
requirement of ₹5,000 crore, the BE has been fixed at ₹2,500 crore, which is 
50% of the projected need. Although, the Ministry has clarified that the BE 
was reduced by the Department of Expenditure based on actual 
expenditure trends from 2021-22 to 2025-26, and additional requirements, if 
any, will be projected at the Revised Estimates/Supplementary Demands 
stage, the Committee feel that such reduced allocations in the final phase 
of the Mission may constrain implementation and delay completion of 
pending works. 
At the same time, in respect of legacy dumpsites, out of 2,510.78 lakh 
metric tonnes (LMT) of identified waste, only 1,568.01 LMT or about 62.5% 
has been remediated and 8,587.67 acres reclaimed, leaving 942.77 LMT yet 
to be treated and 6,671.03 acres of land to be reclaimed. While some 
States/UTs have achieved full remediation, large quantities of waste remain 
pending in States such as Maharashtra, Karnataka, West Bengal, 
Rajasthan, Delhi and Tamil Nadu. The pace of remediation is uneven and 

89 
 
substantial work remains to be completed within a limited timeframe. The 
Committee note that the Ministry has launched the Dumpsite Remediation 
Accelerator Programme (DRAP) on 8th November, 2025, with the aim of 
completing remediation of all dumpsites by 31st March, 2027. 
As the Mission is in its final phase with the goal of making all cities 
“Garbage Free” by 2026, the Committee emphasise that adequate financial 
support and faster remediation of legacy dumpsites are essential for 
achieving this objective. Any delay in addressing funding gaps and 
pending waste treatment may hinder timely completion of the Mission. The 
Committee, therefore, recommend to the Ministry that : 
(i) Adequate and realistic assessment of funds should be made at the 
Budget Estimate stage itself in line with projected requirements and 
physical targets and any drastic reductions at the Revised Estimate 
stage should be avoided; 
(ii) A clear, State/UT-wise time-bound action plan with quarterly targets 
should be prepared to clear the remaining legacy waste under the 
DRAP and special monitoring and support should be provided to 
States where large quantities of waste are still pending;  
(iii) it should be ensured that within two years every ULB has ‘waste 
treatment plants’ (WTPs) with a capacity proportionate to the amount 
of waste generated currently while also envisaging future needs, to 
avoid growth of new dumpsites and landfills; and   
(iv) greater emphasis should be put on sustainable and scientific 
methods such as waste-to-energy, bio-mining, composting and 
material recovery, so that legacy waste is properly processed rather 
than merely shifted. States with large pending quantities should be 
encouraged to adopt value-recovery models to generate energy, 
reduce landfill burden and ensure productive use of reclaimed land. 
 
 
 
 

90 
 
Recommendation No. 9 
Need for Expedited Implementation and Improved Financial Planning under 
PM e-Bus Sewa Scheme 
 
The Committee note that the PM e-Bus Sewa Scheme aims to deploy 
10,000 electric buses with Central Assistance of ₹20,000 crore and is valid 
up to March 2037. Against the target of 10,000 buses, 9,642 buses have 
been sanctioned across 110 cities in 18 States and 5 UTs, out of 178 eligible 
cities. However, only 225 buses have been delivered and made operational 
so far in just four cities viz. Guwahati, Bhavnagar, Nagpur and Chandigarh. 
The Committee also observe that guidelines for Green Urban Mobility 
Initiatives (GUMI) under Segment-B are yet to be finalised, thereby delaying 
implementation of Intelligent Traffic Management System (ITMS) and 
National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) -based Automated Fare Collection 
Systems. 
The Committee further note the repeated gap between Budget 
Estimates, Revised Estimates and actual releases. Against BE of ₹1,300 
crore in 2024–25, the RE was reduced to ₹500 crore, with actual release of 
₹475.44 crore. Similarly, in 2025–26, against BE of ₹1,310 crore, the RE was 
reduced to ₹300 crore, with ₹237.56 crore released as on 19.02.2026. The 
Ministry has attributed these reductions to delays in submission of 
proposals, tendering, infrastructure readiness and operationalisation at the 
State/UT level. 
The Committee emphasise that unless implementation and financial 
utilisation are accelerated, the intended benefits of clean, efficient and 
green public transport may not be realised within the planned timeframe. 
The Committee recommend that the Ministry : 
(i) must ensure time-bound completion of depots, charging and power 
infrastructure so that sanctioned buses are made operational without 
further delay;  
(ii) Prepare a detailed State/UT-wise implementation roadmap with 
defined milestones to cover the remaining eligible cities, ensuring all  
the sanctioned buses are operational at the earliest;  

91 
 
(iii) expedite finalisation and rollout of GUMI guidelines promptly to 
ensure timely implementation of integrated urban mobility 
improvements; and 
(iv) budgetary projections should be prepared on a more realistic 
assessment of States/UT readiness and project execution capacity to 
avoid repeated downward revisions at the RE stage. 
 
Recommendation No. 10 
Assessment of ULB’s vendor carrying capacity for PM SVANidhi 
 
The Committee note that the Pradhan Mantri Street Vendors 
Atmanirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) was launched as a positive intervention 
by the Central Government for members of the lowest strata of urban 
society, namely, the street vendors who were hit hard by the Covid 
Pandemic. One of the tacit achievements of the Scheme was the 
implementation of the Street Vendors Act, 2014 across States/UTs by 
intertwining the requirements of the Scheme with the provisions of the Act. 
Continuing the momentum created by PM SVANidhi in terms of bringing 
street vendors into the fold of formal financial system and also promoting 
digital transactions, in August 2025, the scheme has been extended in a 
restructured manner till 2030 with a budgetary allocation of Rs.900 crore in 
BE 2026-27and Department of Financial Services (DFS) has also been taken 
on board.  
However, the Committee observe that out of 73.33 lakh loans 
disbursed in the first tranche, 28.03 lakh of total disbursed loans are still 
outstanding which is 38.23 percent of the total disbursed loans, indicating 
that 28.03 lakh street vendors are yet to repay their first tranche of loans 
and are not eligible for the second tranche of loan. Further, the Committee 
have also been informed that beneficiary target under the restructured 
scheme is 1.15 crore including 50 lakh new beneficiaries.  
The Committee understand that the scheme is demand driven, 
intending to cover all eligible street vendors willing to avail loans, and 
since the vendor population is dynamic (with new vendors entering & 

92 
 
exiting regularly), the Ministry does not have data on precise number of 
street vendors in the country. Nonetheless, it is important that the scheme 
should not lead to an unintentional surge in the number of street vendors 
in urban areas, thereby further congesting the limited public space or 
vending zones and footpaths. The Committee, thus recommend that  
(i) the Ministry should direct all the States/UTs, through Urban Local 
Bodies (ULBs), to assess the carrying capacity of designated 
vending zones and ULBs managed spaces to determine the number 
of street vendors that can be accommodated at a time and formulate 
a policy in this regard; 
(ii) Further, the ULBs through States/UTs must be strictly directed to 
issue Letter of Recommendation (LoR)/Certificate of Vending (CoV) 
to new vendors for the purpose of availing loan under PM SVANidhi 
only after conducting the stated ‘ULBs vendor carrying capacity 
assessment’ survey/exercise; 
(iii) It should be ensured that vending zones are strategically located in 
high footfall and commercially viable areas, in accordance with the 
Street Vendors Act, and PM SVANidhi guidelines to ensure 
sustainable business opportunities for vendors.  
 
Recommendation No. 11 
Need for Expedited Operationalisation and Effective Utilisation of Funds 
under CITIIS 2.0 
 
The Committee note that CITIIS 2.0 was approved in May 2023 with 
the objective of promoting circular economy–based integrated waste 
management at the city level, climate-oriented reforms at the State level 
and institutional strengthening at the national level. However, despite the 
programme being operational for nearly two years, financial progress 
remains significantly slow. 
Against a proposed outlay of ₹1,139.8 crore for 2026–27, only ₹300 
crore has been allocated. Further, actual expenditure has been minimal, 
i.e., ₹9.25 crore in 2024–25 and ₹0.17 crore in 2025–26, primarily because 

93 
 
the programme is still in the project preparation and maturation phase. The 
Committee also observe that although 18 cities have been selected under 
Component 1, project components and costs are yet to be finalised and 
implementation activities have not commenced. Similarly, under 
Component 2, while Tripartite Agreements have been signed with 21 
States/UTs, fund disbursement is linked to Disbursement Linked Indicators 
(DLIs) and expenditure remains limited. 
The Committee further note that the programme is supported 
through substantial external funding from Agence Française de 
Développement (French Development Agency) (AFD), Kreditanstalt für 
Wiederaufbau ("Credit Institute for Reconstruction") (KfW) and the 
European Union. Although no commitment charges or financial burden 
have arisen so far, continued delays in grounding projects may risk 
inefficient fund utilisation and affect the intended outcomes within the 
stipulated timeframe. 
In view of the above, the Committee recommend that the Ministry: 
(i) should expedite finalisation of project components and cost 
estimates for the 18 selected cities and ensure commencement of 
on-ground implementation with a clearly defined, time-bound 
framework for both city-level and State-level components; 
(ii) should  strengthen coordination with participating States/UTs to fast-
track approvals, procurement and execution, while ensuring that 
budget projections are realistic and aligned with actual 
implementation capacity to avoid persistent under-utilisation and 
wide gaps between outlay and expenditure; and 
(iii) Closely monitor phased drawdown of external loans and strictly link 
it to physical and financial progress so as to ensure timely utilisation 
and prevent any potential financial implications, thereby 
safeguarding the intended objectives of CITIIS 2.0. 
 
 
 

94 
 
 
Recommendation No. 12 
Focus of smaller Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) under the Urban Challenge 
Fund 
In the Budget 2025-2026, the Union Government proposed to set up 
an Urban Challenge Fund of ₹1 lakh crore to implement the proposals 
under three verticals, namely, (i) ‘Cities as Growth Hubs’, (ii) ‘Creative 
Redevelopment of Cities’ and (iii) 'Water and Sanitation'. According to the 
Ministry, this fund will finance up to 25 per cent of the cost of bankable 
projects with a stipulation that at least 50 per cent of the cost is funded 
from the market sources such as bonds, bank loans, and Public-Private 
Partnerships (PPPs) and the remaining 25 percent are financed by States, 
ULBs or through other sources. 
The Committee understand that urban infrastructure requires 
substantial funding, which so far have been supported primarily by 
budgetary grants. The Committee appreciate that against this backdrop, an 
innovative shift has been proposed, aiming to generate ₹4 lakh crore for 
urban development over the next five years through a challenge based, 
market-linked, reform driven and outcome-oriented scheme by 
encouraging States and ULBs to raise funds from the market for financing 
urban infrastructure projects. The Committee have also noted that these 
changes will be accompanied by reforms in accounting system followed by 
States/Cities/ULBs. Further, to enable participation of fiscally weaker Urban 
Local Bodies, a Credit Repayment Guarantee Sub-Scheme has been 
approved under the Urban Challenge Fund. A corpus of ₹5,000 crore has 
been created under this Sub-Scheme to provide credit repayment 
guarantee support. The Sub-Scheme will cover all ULBs in Northeastern 
and Hilly States/UTs and smaller ULBs (with population below 1,00,000) in 
other States/UTs, enabling them to raise resources from the market and 
participate in the Urban Challenge Fund.  
The Committee observe that the Ministry were not able to raise 
desired funds through Public Private Partnership (PPP) under earlier 
Schemes, such as the Smart Cities Mission. Further, the success of any 

95 
 
Scheme depends on the delivery capability and absorption capacity of the 
ULBs. The bigger ULBs will naturally be in a better position to avail 
themselves of the benefits of the UCF compared to the smaller ones. The 
Committee, thus recommend the Ministry :  
(i) to specifically focus on smaller cities and those cities which were 
not covered under the Smart Cities Mission so that the intended 
benefits generated from the Scheme are evenly distributed; and 
(ii) for early finalisation of guidelines and operational modalities of the 
Scheme. 
 
Recommendation No. 13 
Need for Ensuring Prior Approval and Policy Clarity in Rollout of New 
Urban Schemes 
The Committee observe that several major initiatives of the Ministry 
such as the National Urban Digital Mission (NUDM), the Scheme for 
Industrial Housing, the Site Adjacent Factory Employee (SAFE) 
Accommodation under Pradhan Mantri - National Industrial Workers 
Accommodation Scheme (PM-NIWAS), Deendayal Jan Aajeevika (Shehari) 
(DJAY-S) and the proposed Municipal Bonds scheme, are yet to receive 
final approval of the Cabinet. At the same time, substantial budgetary 
allocations have been made in successive years, even though the 
contours, guidelines, funding patterns and implementation frameworks of 
these schemes are still under formulation. 
In the case of NUDM, the Cabinet Note has been returned for revision 
and the Mission framework is under reconsideration, yet allocations were 
provided in 2024-25 and 2025-26 with sharp reductions thereafter at RE 
stage. Similarly, DJAY-S has concluded its pilot phase and awaits Cabinet 
approval for full-scale rollout, while fresh allocations have been made in BE 
2026–27. The Industrial Housing/PM–NIWAS initiative was announced with 
₹2,500 crore in 2025–26 and ₹400 crore in 2026-27, despite the scheme 
remaining at the conceptual stage. The Municipal Bonds scheme has been 
introduced with a token allocation of ₹100 crore even though its guidelines 

96 
 
are under preparation and requisite approvals of the Cabinet and 
Expenditure Finance Committee are pending. 
The Committee feel that announcing schemes, making budgetary 
allocations and even operating pilot projects for indefinite periods without 
final statutory approval and clearly notified guidelines lead to uncertainty 
in implementation, under-utilisation of funds, frequent revisions in budget 
estimates and lack of accountability in outcomes. Such an approach also 
creates confusion among States/UTs and ULBs regarding eligibility, 
funding support and long-term sustainability. Moreover, it may give rise to 
a perception that policy initiatives are characterised more by 
announcements and preliminary allocations than by timely execution on 
the ground. The Committee emphasise that all announced initiatives 
should be implemented promptly so that they translate into tangible 
outcomes and benefits for citizens. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that : 
(i) proper due diligence must be undertaken by the Ministry before 
making full-scale budgetary allocations for any new scheme. 
Allocations should be provided only after the scheme’s contours, 
funding pattern and implementation guidelines have been finalised 
and approved by the competent authority. Any token provision, if 
considered necessary, should be clearly justified and accompanied 
by a defined timeline;  
(ii) Proposals such as NUDM, DJAY-S, Industrial Housing/PM–NIWAS 
and Municipal Bonds, which are currently under consideration for 
approval, should be placed before the Cabinet/EFC at the earliest, 
with a clearly defined timeline for their operational rollout; 
(iii) Pilot initiatives should have clearly defined objectives, evaluation 
frameworks and clauses, and their learnings should be formally 
incorporated into the final scheme design before scaling up. 
 
 
 

97 
 
 
Recommendation No. 14 
Promoting effective coordination and integration among urban sector 
schemes to prevent duplication and overlapping 
 
The Committee observe that multiple schemes of the Ministry 
operate within closely related thematic areas affordable housing for 
workers under Affordable Rental Housing Complexes (ARHCs) under PMAY 
(U) and the Scheme for Industrial Housing/SAFE Accommodation under 
PM–NIWAS; sewage and wastewater management under AMRUT and 
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM-Urban); solid waste management and 
circular economy initiatives under SBM-U and City Investments to 
Innovate, Integrate and Sustain (CITIIS-2.0) and Urban Challenge Fund 
(UCF); and urban livelihoods and employment through PM SVANidhi and 
DJAY-S. While each scheme has distinct objectives, their operational 
domains often intersect at the level of States/UTs and Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs). 
The Committee feel that, in the absence of a clearly articulated 
convergence framework, such overlap may lead to duplication of funding, 
fragmented implementation, inefficient utilisation of resources and 
confusion among implementing agencies and beneficiaries. There is also a 
risk of multiple schemes financing similar infrastructure components or 
targeting overlapping beneficiary groups without proper integration of 
objectives and outcomes. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry to prepare and 
notify a comprehensive convergence framework clearly delineating the 
scope, target beneficiaries, admissible components and funding patterns 
of each urban sector scheme so as to prevent overlap, promote 
complementarities and ensure optimal utilisation of public resources; 
 
 
 

98 
 
Recommendation No. 15 
Need for Long-Term Urban Infrastructure Planning and Investment Strategy 
 
  The Committee sought to ascertain whether the Ministry has 
prepared or proposes to prepare a unified long-term urban strategy aligned 
with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, integrating infrastructure creation, 
governance reforms, climate resilience, economic growth and social 
inclusion across metropolitan, Tier-II and Tier-III cities. The Committee have 
been apprised that the High Powered Expert Committee (HPEC), in its 2011 
report, had estimated urban infrastructure investment requirements up to 
2031 and projected urban population share to increase to 75% by 2030. 
Since then, no similar Committee has been constituted. The Ministry further 
referred to the 2022 report “Cities as Engines of Growth” by NITI Aayog and 
Asian Development Bank (ADB), which highlights the strong correlation 
between urbanisation and GDP growth. The Ministry submitted that various 
ongoing missions such as AMRUT 2.0, SBM-U 2.0, PMAY-U 2.0, Metro Rail 
Projects and PM e-Bus Seva are contributing towards improving quality of 
life and supporting the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. 
 
  The Committee note that while several flagship schemes are being 
implemented and financing support mechanisms have been introduced, 
these interventions are largely scheme-driven and sector-specific. The last 
comprehensive and consolidated assessment of urban infrastructure 
requirements was undertaken by the HPEC in 2011, with projections only 
up to 2031. No updated national-level assessment has been undertaken to 
estimate infrastructure demand, financing gaps and institutional 
requirements beyond 2030 in a holistic manner. Given the rapid pace of 
urbanisation, the growing economic centrality of cities, emerging climate 
risks and the stated national goal of achieving ‘Viksit Bharat 2047’, the 
absence of an integrated long-term urban investment and strategy 
framework may lead to fragmented planning, sub-optimal allocation of 
resources and financing stress in the future. 

99 
 
 
  In view of the above, the Committee recommend the Ministry to 
constitute a new High-Level Expert Committee to comprehensively assess 
India’s urban infrastructure requirements, financing needs, governance 
reforms and capacity-building imperatives up to 2047 aligned with the 
vision of ‘Viksit Bharat 2047’. A forward-looking and evidence-based 
roadmap would enable coordinated planning, better fiscal preparedness 
and balanced urban development across metropolitan, Tier-II and Tier-III 
cities. 
 
 
 
      Shri Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy

2. At the outset, the Chairperson welcomed the Members of the Committee and the 
representatives of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, NBCC, HUDCO, Delhi Jal 
Board and Municipal Corporation of Delhi to the Sitting of the Committee convened to 
take oral evidence on the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Housing and Urban 
Affairs for the Financial Year 2026-27.  In his opening remarks, the Chairperson sought 
the reasons for downward revision of Ministry’s grants at the RE stage in the Financial 
Year 2025-26 by nearly forty percent and its impact on the vision of ‘Viksit Bharat by 
2047’. He also sought the reasons for delay in receiving the Cabinet nod for various 
Schemes announced in the previous Budgets and have also received budgetary 
allocations.  
3. The Secretary, MoHUA briefed the Committee about the vision and plans for 
planned urbanisation during the year 2026 and the years thereafter. He pointed out that 
the issue of shortage of funds for urban infrastructure has now been addressed and since 
2024 there has been a consistent growth in the budgetary allocation of the Ministry. The 
representatives of the Ministry further informed the Committee that the focus of the 
Budget 2026-27 is on developing the infrastructure of cities with over 5 lakh population 
through mapping of city economic regions, establishing a reform-cum-results based 
financing mechanism and encouraging issuance of Municipal Bonds of higher value for 

105 
 
larger cities. It was followed by a power-point presentation highlighting the challenges in 
urban space, budgetary overview and financial statistics, scheme-wise allocation, 
progress made under various schemes of the Ministry, SSASCI reforms and the way 
ahead.  
4. The Members, thereafter,  raised several issues such as slower pace of expenditure, 
issue of conversion of unoccupied dwellings in Delhi under Affordable Rental Housing 
Scheme, alternate scheme for re-settling slums occupying Railway land or reserved 
forest-hilly land which could not be covered under In-situ Slum Redevelopment vertical, 
formulation and updation of guidelines related to street vendors to regulate street vending 
and vending zones, location of affordable housing projects in the outskirts of the city, 
enhancement of centre’s share for a dwelling unit under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojna 
(Urban) (PMAY(U), preservation of urban forest, deteriorated quality of drinking water 
in metro cities. Matter regarding glaring vacancies in Urban Local Bodies, prevention of 
leakage in urban water supply system, need for enhancement of road infrastructure to 
match the rising vehicular and human population in a city, lower spending under 
SBM(U), slow progress of Mumbai Metro Line 6 (Pink Line), better monitoring of 
various schemes of MoHUA, status of MetroLite and MetroNeo projects, were also 
raised.  The Committee also emphasized need of mandatory Sewage Treatment Plant 
(STP) in every city, creation of energy from waste to avoid the problem of rising 
dumpsites/landfills, developing a smart water drain system to recoup underground water. 
The concept and modalities of Urban Challenge Fund was also discussed in detail.  
5. The representatives of the Ministry answered to the various queries/concerns 
raised by the Members.  
6. To conclude, the Hon’ble Chairperson thanked the witnesses for inputs provided 
by them on the subject and directed them that any pending information not readily 
available during the sitting be submitted to the Committee Secretariat, in writing, at the 
earliest. 
The Committee then adjourned till the next sitting

I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Industry,  having   been  
authorised  by the  Committee, hereby present this 100 th Report of  Sub-Committee-I for  Ministry of Steel and Mines (
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry)  on  Performance Review  of  National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) which is under the administrative control of  Ministry of Steel .
2.The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee-I for Ministry of Steel and Mines .  The Sub-Committee took
up the issue of Performance Review of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC)). The Sub-
Committee visited Hyderabad  from 28th and 29th June , 2002 and interacted with the  management of National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
3.            The Report has been prepared on  the basis of   on the spot  study and  interaction with the    Secretary ,
Ministry of Steel and officials  of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
4          The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 17th  December, 2002  considered and adopted  the  Report. 
5.         The Committee at its meeting held on 17th December,  2002 considered and adopted the Report.         
 
NEW DELH
December   17, 2002   
                                      
 DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman

REPORT
 
National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini
Ratna Category-I” Company was established  in the year 1958, in pursuance of Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 to
promote and undertake development of minerals (other than coal, oil and atomic minerals) in Public Sector. NMDC is
the largest producer and exporter of iron ore in this Country. Its exports are around 7 million tonnes of iron ore per
annum (through Minerals & Metals Trading Corporation Ltd - canalising agency). It has also exported about 1.7 MT of

iron ore directly to China in 2001-02. NMDC has earned approximately Rs.750 Crores during the year 2001-02 by way
of foreign exchange. NMDC has been consistently achieving the rating of “ Excellent” from the very first year of
signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92,
from which it moved to third rank in the year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s
performance of excellence and the achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU
performance evaluation, NMDC has been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This unique achievement,
as the Joint Top Rank,   has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98,
1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “Excellent”, barring 1998-99 during which period there
was general recession.

company might improve over the figure  of last year.

10.0     COST COMPONENTS OF PRODUCTS PRODUCEDBY NMDC .
 
10.1     The main components of the cost of production are  Fixed Cost and  Variable Cost.
The fixed cost consists of salaries and wages, depreciation and office/ selling expenses. The fixed cost is being reduced
by introduction of multi-skilling concepts and by adoption of CCTV at OCSL Plants. The variable cost consists of
explosives, drill bits, tyre & tubes, spares and consumables. It also consists cost incurred towards royalty and
electricity. 
 
10.2     The cost of production at pit head is comparable with the International Mining Operations. NMDC has to incur
additional Railway freight and Port handling charges  before product reaches the consumer. The port charges and
Railway freight charges are not under the control of NMDC. It may be worth mentioning that the cost incurred in
Railway freight and port charges amounts to 60% of the cost and balance 40% cost is in the control of NMDC. This
situation creates difficulty for NMDC to compete in the  international market for iron ore. Unless efforts are made to
reduce the railway freight and port charges, it will be difficult for NMDC to sustain the progress of the Corporation. 
 
10.3     Continuous efforts are being made towards cost reduction through the various managerial controls such as
 
a.
       Bench Marking
b.      Incentive for maintaining electricity and diesel consumption targets adopted through the Memorandum of
Understanding reached between management and union.
c.       Standard Costing
d.      Continuous review of consumables and improvement in the same
 
10.4     The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC management has introduced the multi-skilling concept to reduced
the fixed cost .    The Committee also notes that various managerial controls measures are at work to reduce the cost of

12.0     MOU RATING OF NMDC 
 
12.1     NMDC is one of the Public Sector Enterprises which has been signing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
with the Government of India since 1991. At the beginning of each financial year, an agreement is reached to achieve
certain parameters such as production, sales, gross margin, ratio of net profit to capital employed, energy conservation,
R & D efforts, human resource development, project implementation etc. based on the past performance into account,
the growth need and the potential to achieve such levels of performance.  These achievements at the year end are
evaluated for the said parameters and the company gets ranked based on the evaluation score. NMDC has been
consistently achieving the rating of “ EXCELLENT” from the very first year of signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was
placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92, from which it moved to third rank in the
year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s performance of excellence and the
achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU performance evaluation, NMDC has
been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This has been a unique achievement as the Joint Top Rank  
has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98, 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and
2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “EXCELLENT”, barring 1998-99 during which period there was general recession. 
NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production, despatches of iron ore, production and
sales of diamonds, profits, increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has been consistently scaling new
heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including foreign exchange earnings to
the country.   For the year 2001-2002, the company has surpassed the MOU target of dispatches of 180 lakh tonnes of
iron ore by achieving 182.04 lakh tonnes. The company has achieved an ever highest profit before tax of Rs.320.15
crores during 2001-2002.
 
12.2     NMDC has achieved the "Excellent" rating during the last five years except in the year 1998-99 which was
"Very Good"due to recession in the international steel industry. DPE has awarded NMDC an award for Excellence in
the achievement of MOU Targets for the year 2000-01 and a certificate of Excellence in the achievement of MOU

19.0     LEGAL FRAMEWORK  FOR GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT OF MINING         OPERATION.
 
19.1     To what extent the existing legal framework is conducive to the growth and development of mining operation.
Any suggestion on the part of NMDC management for legal reform in this regard is as follow:-
 
“Mineral industry is governed by certain statutory act and rules such  as  Mines and Mineral Development and
Regulation Act, Mineral Conservation and Development Rules,  Mineral Concession Rule, , Mines Act etc.  With the 
economic liberalization, a new National  Mineral Policy  was announced in 1993 in which 13  major minerals were
dereserved and also foreign investment in the mineral industry was encouraged.  With the existing change in the legal
frame work, State Governments have been empowered to grant and renew mining lease as  minerals are considered to
be property of  the  concerned States.  However, it is observed that State Govts. are imposing their own conditions in
granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral industry.  State
Governments should be advised to  form uniform policy and grant mining/prospecting lease on first come first basis,
rather than tendering, asking  for  additional royalty etc.
 
19.2     Ministry of Mines in consultation with GSI & IBM identify mineral zones, which should be developed to meet
the country’s need and such mineral zones, which should be developed to meet the country’s need and such mineral
zones should be taken out from the purview of Forest Conservation Act. “
 
19.3     The Committee is anguished  to  note the  submission of NMDC management  that  State Govts. are imposing
their own conditions in granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral
industry and asking  for sweet equity, additional royalty etc.
 
 
 
19.4     The Committee is of the view that  procedural hurdles and bureaucratic rest-redtapism  should not  come onto
the way of systematic development of mineral industry.
 
19.5     The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should   approach the Department of Mines for
organizing  across the  table interaction of representatives of   mineral enterprises and  officials of state  Government  to
form uniform mineral policy as per the canons of National Mineral Policy 1993 and  sort out problems relating  to
granting of  mining/prospecting lease etc.    The Committee  feels that the Department of Mines should  issue direction 
to GSI and IBM for identification of `Exclusive Mineral Zones’ for systematic exploration and exploitation of  Mineral
resources.  Having been give due weightage  to environmental aspects, `exclusive Mineral zones may be taken out from
the  purview of forest   conservation Act.

21.0     'Pricing policy' of NMDC
 
21.1     NMDC is supplying iron ore in the domestic market as well as for export purposes.  The iron ore, which is
surplus to the domestic demand, is exported to countries like Japan, China and South Korea.  The main export of
NMDC’s ore is through MMTC as per the existing EXIM policy.  However, NMDC is also exporting small quantities of
iron ore directly based on the specific export license issued by the Ministry of Commerce / DGFT.
 
21.2     Export Prices ; The prices for export of iron ore are basically determined by the global demand and supply
position on year-to-year basis. The percentage increase/decrease in prices over the previous year is usually finalized
between the major exporters of iron ore like Australia and Brazil and major importers like Japan and European
countries.  The same percentage increase/decrease in prices is made applicable to the exports from India.  Consequently
the prices of NMDC iron ore is also decided on the same basis. 
           
21.3     Domestic Prices: The despatches to domestic market accounts for about 53% of the total dispatches of NMDC’s
iron ore.  The dispatches to domestic market are regulated in terms of long-term agreement signed by various domestic
customers.  The duration of the agreement is for a maximum period of 5 years.  Iron ore market has remained basically a
buyers market due to frequent and prolonged recessionary trends in the steel industry.  Therefore the fixed escalation in
prices is not the acceptable norm in the industry.  In terms of the long-term agreement the prices of iron ore are to be
settled each year by mutual discussions.  The mutual discussions to finalise the prices instills a sense of confidence
among the buyers that NMDC is sensitive to the customer’s needs.
 
21.4     The Board of Directors of NMDC delegated the powers for deciding the pricing through an internal committee
consisting of CMD, Director (Prdn), Director (Fin) and ED (Comml.) and authorizing CMD to take up action as deemed
necessary in this regard.
21.,5    In terms of the above decision of the Board, negotiations are held by NMDC with the parties concerned in the
beginning of the each financial year.  The negotiation are primarily based upon the “what the market can bear” criteria,
and the ground realities of steel sector.  The negotiation also to some extent take into consideration the global
demand/supply position and trends of iron ore prices in the international market. 
 
21.6     The prices so negotiated and finalized with the parties are put up for the information of the Board and adopted
for supplies during the relevant year.

 21.11.0           NEED OF   AUTONOMY FOR  NMDC IN EXPORT PROMOTION I.E.                               
DIRECT EXPORT BY NMDC
 
 
 21.11.1 The export of iron ore produced by NMDC is canalized through MMTC Ltd. in terms of the existing EXIM
policy.  The iron ore which is surplus to the demand of domestic industry is offered for export.  The major chunk of
export is canalised through MMTC and balance uncommitted quantity is permitted for exports directly by NMDC
through special export license.  The inherent drawback of the system are as follows:
 
                        (i)      The licenses issued to NMDC for exports by DGFT do not permit export to major importers of Iron Ore
like Japan and South Korea which together accounts for about 40 - 45% of sea-borne trade.
 
                      (ii)      The licenses are for limited quantity with a validity period of two/three years.  Therefore it is not possible
for NMDC to enter into an agreement/MOU on long-term basis with foreign buyers.
 
                     (iii)      NMDC has to ensure the parity of foreign exchange realization on exports on product-to-product basis with
MMTC.  Thus NMDC is deprived the freedom to adjust the prices etc. depending upon the available
inventory levels vis-à-vis the demand pattern.
 
                    (iv)      The import license imposes the restriction on NMDC to export to Japan and South Korea but for other
countries both MMTC and NMDC will be trading the same product and the brand image of the NMDC
product will never be established.
 
                      (v)      Since NMDC gets permission for Direct Export on piece-meal basis, the foreign steel mills operators have
reservations to consider NMDC as a long-term reliable supplier of iron ore.
 
                    (vi)      Since the Export Licenses are for limited quantities, NMDC cannot offer the whole product mix comprising
of both lump ore and fine ore as required by end users.
 
21.11.2            Therefore in the best interest of exports, NMDC should have complete autonomy and be permitted to
export its iron ore without any restriction of quantity, quality or geographical location.  This will enable NMDC to
operate more like any commercial organization and take business decision, which are in its best interest
 
21.11.3            NMDC is meeting the domestic demand of iron ore to an extent of 55% and the remaining 45% only is
being sold out to international market.  As per the policy of the government iron ore is to be exported through canalising
agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to iron ore with 65% Fe content and above, whereas NMDC has got more
quantity of iron ore lying at pit head with less than 65% Fe content for which international market is available, but not
explored by NMDC.   To take care of this product NMDC is requesting Commerce Ministry to allow NMDC to direct
export to the countries other than the purchasers from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pakistan and South Korea. NMDC has already
exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 lakh tonnes in 1999-00, 9.65 lakh tonnes in 2000-01and  17.12 lakh tonnes in

23.1     Keeping pace with the national policy on workers’ participation in industry, NMDC has made a remarkable

irrespective of their recognition by the labour machinery, affiliation to different  Central Trade Unions, participate as

issues relating to job specifications, work atmosphere and other service matters are settled amicably during the

25.1  Inflated mileage on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line.
 
25.1.1.Railways have been charging freight on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line (SE Railway) by inflating the distance by 30%
NMDC has been representing for the removal of the same in view of the increased traffic handled on the line. The
inflation in distance on K-K line had been continuing since 1967. Initially it was 65.2% but with the traffic volume
increasing, this was reduced to 30% in 1981. This percentage of inflation has been continuing since then. In the last
eighteen years there has been significant increase in the traffic handled on K-K line originating iron ore movement has
gone up from 56.36 lakh tonnes in 1987-88 to 145 lakh tonnes in 2000-01. In addition, the line has been handling other
traffic particularly on account of the NALCO's alumina plant near Koraput. In addition to the budgetary increase in the
freight charges over the years since 1981, Railways had been revising the classification of iron ore upwards resulting in
further increasing in the freight charges. The classification of iron ore which was 110 in 1989-90 had increased to 120 in
1994-95 and 125 in 1999-2000. For the year 2001-02, the Railway freight in respect of iron ore has been further
increased by 3% over that of the previous year with the classification remaining unchanged at 120.
 
25.1.2  The reduction in inflated mileage would help both NMDC and other domestic customers like VSP, Essar Steel,
Ispat Industries Ltd and Vikram Ispat to improve their economy in the operations.
 
25.1.3  The Sub-Committee was informed  that the Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. is linked to  Balladilla Mines of NMDC
for sourcing its iron  ore  requirements.  The  Kothavalasa-Kirandul section (  KK Line) under  Waltair Division of S.E.
Railway measures a distance of 475 kms.  Out of this distance, 118 k.m. is  on the Eastern Ghat Section and the balance
distance is in the plains  or  plateau.  This was constructed at a  cost of Rs159 Crore. and  was  opened for traffic in 
November, 1968.  In the initial stages,  Railways levied freight charges by  inflating the distance by 65.2 percent  with
stipulation  that the freight should be levied  on discontinuous  mileage basis (i.e.)  out of  475 k.m., only 35 km (i.e.)
from Kothavalala to VSP  will be charged normal freight.  Upon a further review in  1981, the percentage of  inflation
on the total distance was reduced to 30 percent  with effect from 1.6.1981. VSP is opereating from 1989 and since then
the inflated freight charge is being levied.  VSP has  transported 463.91 lakh tonnes upto March, 2002 and paid a freight
of Rs.1634.34 crore .Had VSP paid normal freight  (i.e.)  Rs.1284 crore  paid upto 2001-02 , VSP would have saved

25.1.6  During the last 10 years, VSP has been requesting in various coordination meetings held by Ministry of Steel or

freight  charge formed a part of the chapter on " assistance from the Government" in MOUs  signed with RINL.
 
25.1.7  In the meeting of  the Sub-Committee  held on 12
th September, 2001 on the subject of "Key Concern Areas of
Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge 
was  discussed in detailed.  Participating in discussion  Shri R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board  expressed his
views :-
 
" On the questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to consider any request from any
manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and which in turn would help the Railways.  But Sir, by
reducing our revenue, we cannot help anyone.  If they are prepared to give us  an undertaking that  if we  reduce the
freight on the KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much  of extra  traffic, we can consider
it."
 
25.1.8  Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed   his opinion in following words:-
 
" The question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of iron ore from Bailadilla,
which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant.  It has a very long history.    It is not really a question of incremental traffic.  The
operative issue here is that 65 per cent additional freight charge was put at a certain  point  of time because that line was
specifically created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point  B,  with an understanding that if the level of
freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would   be removed.  The  situation today is that, as against the 65
per cent  enhanced rate that was being charged, the  current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic  generated on
that line, today,  12 tonnes. We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on.  We understand that
at a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in order to make it viable
for the Railways.  Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has been achieved, the incremental rate should not
apply.  That was the original understanding.  One cannot have a situation wherein because  there is an incremental rate,
in order to reduce it, you must have incremental traffic.  The fact  that rate was brought down from 65 per cent  to 35 per
cent and now to 30 per cent is, itself, a recognition of the  understanding on which this 65 per cent  was  charged.  Now,
as per that understanding, that additionally factor should now go.  This  is the issue that has to be examined.
 
25.1.9  Responding to the arguments of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-
 
            " The Additionally which was charged earlier was for several reasons.  The first reason was that because it was a
hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost of rails was very high.  The second reason was that we had
put surcharge on  movement of any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is
normally required on a  plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place .  So, the cost of operation also was very
high.   Also, the  electricity  bill for the  operational  of  this line is five times higher than what it would cost in the case
of   a line on the plain.  Now, how do we recover that cost ?  We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a
commitment on the part of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra steel and thus give us that much
of extra traffic.".

MAJOR CUSTOMERS OF NMDC IN DOMESTIC AND FOREIGN MARKET AND NEED OF AUTONOMY
FOR NMDC IN EXPORT PROMOTION I.E. DIRECT EXPORT BY NMDC
 
The Committee notes that NMDC sells 55% of its production for the domestic market while 45%  is being sold
out  to   international  market.   The  Committee wonders that even in the age of liberalization and  globalisation the
Government continues with policy of  allowing  the service  of canalizing agency.  De-canalisation should have
followed the liberalization policy.  While decanalisation  applies with one of PSUs under the Ministry of Steel i.e. Metal
Scrap Trade Corporation  Limited (MSTC) and the same principle has  not been  applied in the case of NMDC.  As per
the existing system, Iron-Ore is to be exported through canalizing agency  i.e.  MMTC.  MMTC finds out market to Iron
ore with 65%  fe content and above whereas NMDC has got  more quantity of Iron Ore lying in  its pit head with less
than fifty-five percent Iron content for which international market  is available but the same is not explored by NMDC. 
Therefore, the Committee feels that, It would  be in the fitness of things that NMDC is given complete  autonomy in the
best – interest of the Company.  The Committee feels NMDC be allowed to direct export to the countries other than the
purchaser from MMTC  i.e. Japan, Pak and South Korea, NMDC has already exported directly to its foreign buyers 
1.27 lakh tones in 1999-2000, 9.65 lakh tones in 2000-01, and  thus experience  so gained, would proved handy to
NMDC in direct export of Iron-ore.
 
( Para : 21.11.4)

present this One Hundred and First Report on the Action Taken on the recommendations contained in the 72nd Report of the Department-related

Para 2.5
ALLOCATION OF FUNDS
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to face the competition, because of their obsolete
R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should
infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into potentially viable PSEs so as to make these ‘Modern Temples’ capable to face the
private sector MNCs in the consumer economy.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The strategies for strengthening and improving the potentially viable PSEs include:---
           1.    Revival of PSEs through BIFR.
           2.    Financial restructuring wherever appropriate.
           3.    Joint Venture formation to have continuous access to technology, finance and marketing.
           4.    Manpower rationalization.
        Out of 26 BIFR referred PSUs under the Department of Heavy Industry revival plans have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. These
involve cash infusion of Rs.654 crore by the Government besides financial restructuring of Rs.2106 crores. Apart from BIFR sanctioned revival
plans, Government has on its own, approved the financial restructuring in case of 7 other sick/loss making PSUs involving fresh infusion of funds to
the extent of Rs.531 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.1443 crores.
        In order to rationalize the manpower, Government have provided an amount of about Rs.1700 crores under Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)
for retiring about 70,000 employees of PSUs.
        Lagan Jute Machinery Co. Ltd. (LJMC), a subsidiary of Bharat Bhari Udyog Nigam Ltd. (BBUNL) and Belting division of Andrew Yule & Co.
Ltd. have already been converted into joint venture companies. Also in case of 30 PSUs of Department of Heavy Industry, the process of JV
formation/disinvestments has been initiated.
Para 2.6
RECOMMENDATION
        In the wake of growing financial crunch in many of the Central PSEs, the Committee recommends that the Government should provide financial
assistance in the form of working capital, Non-plan loan, Government guarantee, etc. to PSEs which are potentially viable.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        Government has been providing financial assistance to the needy PSEs for the working capital (e.g. salary and wages, employees related dues
etc.) and VRS/VSS as non-plan loans. The funds released during the last three years are as follows:---

1999-2000 446.34
2000-2001 637.98
2001-2002 787.04
(Company-wise details given in Annexure-I).
        Government is also giving guarantees for raising loans from the Financial Institution for meeting their working capital requirement etc. Total
sum guaranteed by the Government for various PSEs as on March, 31,.2002 is Rs.1333.20 crore.
Para 2.9
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that while rationalising the Government equity in non-strategic PSEs, interests of the workers should be protected
fully.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The Government is fully alive to the need to protect the interests of the workers. Provisions in the Shareholder agreements generally incorporate
the following clauses regarding employee protection.
        1.     The parties envision that all employees of the Company on the date thereof shall continue in the employment of the Company.
        2.     The Company shall not retrench any part of its labour force for a stipulated period from the closing date other than any dismissal or
termination of employees of the Company from their employment in accordance with the standing orders/disciplinary rules of the Company.

        The Committee notes that cess funds have been utilized over the years to strengthen the infrastructure of the research institutes Automotive

components to meeting regulations relating to safety and emission norms. The Committee recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should

        Funds to meet the full requirement of the six closed PSEs i.e. Mining and Allied Machinery Corporation (MAMC), Bharat Process and
