Para 6.2
GUARANTEE FEE SUBSIDY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that the Department of Heavy Industry has provided for the provision of guarantee fee subsidy to only four
PSEs in 2001-02 leaving most of the needy PSEs to face hardships in getting bank finance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should provide guarantee fee subsidy to the needy PSEs for leveraging finance for sustaining their operations.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        It may be mentioned that Government has already given guarantees to number of PSEs under DHI for cash credit facilities from Banks/Financial
Institutions for meeting working capital requirements. The total sum guaranteed by the Government for various PSEs under DHI as on March 31,
2002 is Rs.1333.20 crore. The guarantee fee is only 1% of the guarantee given. The guarantee fee subsidy provided to Hindustan Cables Ltd., Burn
Standard Company Ltd. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd. And Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. Mentioned in the para was as per the approved
revival schemes of these PSEs. A new scheme was also introduced in 2000-01 for providing interest subsidy on bank finance to PSEs, for
implementation of VRS. As per this scheme, 50% of the interest due on funds raised through bonds for VRS is disbursed as interest subsidy to the
PSEs concerned, which is much higher than the guarantee fee subsidy. However, guarantee fee subsidy as approved by the Government in the revival
plans of the PSEs, will continue to be provided.
Para 6.6 ---- 6.7
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that under this new scheme introduced by DHI, more funds should be given to Richardson & Cruddas (R&C),
Tung Bhadra Steel Products Ltd. (TSPL), Triveni Structurals Ltd, Instrumentation Ltd, Burn Standard Company Ltd (BSCL) and Hindustan Cables
Ltd. (HCL). To so as to meet their demands to finance manpower rationalisation programme undertaken in these PSEs.
        The Committee further recommends that in case the amount earmarked is not sufficient for this purpose, the additional allocations may be
sought at RE stage.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        A Budget provision of Rs.10 crore was made in BE 2000-01 for interest subsidy on Bank Finance to PSEs for raising funds from
Banks/Financial Institutions for VRS in order to reduce the burden on the Companies. The initial response from the PSEs was not quite encouraging
as the scheme represented a marked departure from the prevailing practice of extending full budgetary support for VRS. Hence the provision was
reduced to Rs.1 crore at RE stage. Out of that provision of Rs.1 crore, only Rs.44.37 lakh could be utilized by one PSE viz., Richardson and Cruddas.
A budget provision per Rs. 20 crore was made in 2001-02 for this purpose. There was good response from the PSEs and a total amount of  Rs. 21.28
crore i.e. Rs. 1.28 crore more than the budget provision was released (HMT – Rs. 20.71 crore, Richardson and Cruddas – Rs. 0.25 crore and
Tungabhadra Steel Products – Rs. 0.32 crore). Consequent of this better response, the budget provision has been enhanced to Rs. 25 crore in BE
2002-03. Out of this provision an amount of Rs. 10.03 crore has already been released in the first quarter of the financial year 2002-03 to Richardson
and Cruddas (Rs. 0.25 crore), Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels Ltd.  (Rs. 0.86 crore) and HMT (Rs. 8.92 crore). Funds will be released to the PSEs as
and when the demand is received. However, if need arises, additional funds will be sought at RE stage or by way of supplementary demands for
grants at the appropriate time.
Para 7.2
PLAN INVESTMENT IN PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that keeping in view the restructuring/revival schemes going on in various PSEs, the Government has
allocated a meager amount of Rs.100.00 crores as Budgetary Support. The Committee, therefore, recommends that additional allocation, if any, may
be considered at RE stage keeping in view the requirements of the respective PSEs.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The plan allocation of Rs. 100 crores as budgetary support to this Department would be sufficient for meeting the presently estimated
requirements of PSEs. As in the previous years, additional funds will be sought at RE stage for any additional demands due to restructuring during the
course of the year.
Para 8.1
NON PLAN LOANS TO PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES
RECOMMENDATION
        Since a number of PSEs are running under losses, the Committee is of the view that the allocated amount of Rs.150.00 crores for revival
schemes and Rs.250.00 crores for VSS and payment of statutory dues may not be sufficient to meet the requirements of large number of PSEs. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that additional allocations, if required, may be made at the RE stage.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        In case the budget provisions of Rs. 150 crore for revival schemes and Rs. 250 crore for VSS/VRS and payment of statutory dues fall short of
the demands of the PSEs, additional allocation for the purpose will be sought at RE stage through supplementary demands for grants.
Para 9.2
BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICALS LIMITED (BHEL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee views BHEL as ‘Hallmark’ of the DHI which is the only PSE under the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises
paying highest dividend to the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while reducing the Government’s stake in BHEL from 66%
to 51%, interests of the workers and Company should be given due consideration.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for consideration at the appropriate time.

HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION LTD. (HPC)
RECOMMENDATION

        Government has been extending budgetary support to Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited (HPC) for meeting plan outlay. Plan Budgetary

Government.
               (b)   Till such time as the arrangement proposed in para (iv) and (vii) below materializes, adjustment of the temporary accommodation
provided by HPC to its subsidiaries for payment of salary and wages beyond March 31, 2000 against HPC’s dues to Government of

        (iii)   Redemption of Non-cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares of Rs. 106.68 crore on March 30,2008 and reissue of the same in favour of

HINDUSTAN MACHINE TOOLS LTD.
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee has noted that the Government has decided to close down 5 unviable units of HMT under its restructuring programme. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should give impetus to the schemes/programmes for training and rehabilitation of retired workers
under VRS/VSS.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        As per the Turn around Plan approved during August 2000 the identified unviable units have been closed except Food Processing Machinery
Unit at Aurangabad (FPA) which has been attached to the Tractor Business. The manpower of the closed units has been offered VRS/and some of
them have been deployed in other units. Department of Public Enterprises implements scheme for training and rehabilitation of workers who avail
VRS/VSS in association with concerned PSUs.
Para 12.2
RAJASTHAN ELECTRONICS AND INSTRUMENTS LTD. (REIL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee views REIL as a potentially viable PSE, which needs fresh infusion of funds so as to update its R&D and projects. The
Committee is, therefore, in conformity with the DHI to invite a joint venture partner for the Company.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        REIL, Jaipur, was incorporated on August 12, 1981 as a Joint Venture between Instrumentation Limited, Kota (ILK); a Public Sector
Undertaking (PSU), under the Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) and Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation
Limited, Jaipur (RIICO), with 51% to 49% ratio. Government interest in REIL is through the shareholding in REIL, as the Government holds 100%
equity in ILK. REIL is earning profits since inception.
        In principle decision has since been taken by this Department to sell and transfer 51% of the equity of ILK in REIL to a Joint Venture (JV)
partner and the process of disinvestments already initiated.
Para 13.4
HINDUSTAN CABLES LTD. (HCL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is happy to note that with the concerted efforts of the Government by applying restructuring plan, the Company’s decline has
stopped and its turnover increased from Rs.203.00 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs.975.00 crores in 2000-01. The Committee feels that this record turnover
of the Company has been possible mainly due to ‘reservation of orders’ for the Company by the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Government should continue making provisions of work orders for the Company.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        Following the package of assistance, which inter-alia  included reservation of orders, the Company increased the turnover from Rs.221 crore in
1998-99 to Rs.803 crore in 1999-2000 and to Rs.875 crore in 2000-01. The reservation of orders was initially for a period of 2 years. The Cabinet
Committee on Disinvestment in its meeting held on February 1, 2001, however, decided for continuation of current reservation of 25% of the annual
requirement of telecom cables of BSNL/MTNL along with 50% advance in favour of the Company till disinvestments and reservation for a further
period of two years after disinvestments.

Para 9.8 – 9.10
PRICE PREFERENCE TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers are not able to avail price preference of 15% for projects funded by
international agencies like World Bank, United Nations, Asian Development Bank etc. as imports on such projects is allowed at ‘nil’ duty as per
Notification No.85/99-customs dated July 6, 1999. The power projects for 10th and 11th Five Year Plans are being finalised. Some of these projects
may entail multilateral funding. Additional power projects of 60,000 MW during the 11 th plan period are likely to be finalised. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Customs Notification No. 85/99 – custom dated July 6, 1999 should be rescinded to enable domestic manufacturers to
effectively compete against foreign suppliers by taking advantage of 15% price preference provided in ICB tenders.
        The Committee views this issue very seriously since it has effected zero customs duty regime applicable to all goods imported to India for
execution of projects financed by the United Nations/World Bank or any other International Organisation. This amended custom duty structure has
adversely affected competitiveness of the domestic Capital Goods industries.
        The Committee, therefore, recommends that this anomaly needs to be rectified at the earliest possible. The Committee also recommends that if
need arises then the DHI should take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) to resolve the log jam. The Committee
further recommends that the unresolved matter may be placed before the Cabinet Committee to consider the matter de-novo.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        This matter has been discussed in the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee. They had constituted a separate Committee headed
by Revenue Secretary for making recommendations on this issue. They have since given their recommendations stating that World Bank guidelines
provide for giving preferential treatment to domestic bidders. Their recommendations were discussed in a meeting on 12.08.2002 by the Standing
Committee (Sub-Committee-III). Further action on these recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee for issue of clarifications is
being taken by the Department of Revenue.
Para 9.11
REFUND OF TERMINAL EXCISE DUTY TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRIES
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, and high cost
of finance and infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports. At present custom duty on Coal Mining, Fertilizer
and Power projects is 5% basic custom duty+16% CVD and ‘nil’ SAD. Under this structure the domestic industry is unable to claim refund of excise
duty and become uncompetitive. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be no duty free import of projects and a minimum of 15%
basic custom duty + ‘nil’ CVD + 4% SAD be imposed to enable the domestic industry to become competitive without increasing the project cost.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The issue has already been taken up by DHI with Ministry of Finance vide D.O. letter No. 3(23)/99-PE.XI dated December 29,.2000. Hon’ble
Minister (HI & PE) vide D.O. letter dated December 23, 2000 has also taken up various issues including the above with Hon’ble Finance Minister
(copy enclosed) (Annexure-VII).

        The Committee regrets to note that despite persistent efforts, the issue of refund of Terminal Excise Duty has  not been resolved. Terminal

those Central PSEs/Companies whose cycle time for completion of the Projects is normally 3 to 4 years. With the withdrawl of this refund, the Power
Companies are unable to absorb the 16% excise duty which is quite substantial. This has been affecting adversely the functioning of all power
companies and particularly the BHEL. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Government/DGFT should make a special measure
for refund of Terminal Excise Duty for those projects/bids, which were finalized (under International Competitive Bidding) before March 31, 2000
for maintaining the continuity of the existing EXIM Policy for projects/bids affected.

        This issue had earlier been taken up with DGFT upon the request of domestic Heavy Electrical Industry and the recommendations of the Sub-
Committee-III. DGFT have informed this Department that they are not in favour of extending the benefit of refund of Terminal Excise Duty if the
supplies have been effected on or after April 1, 2000, even if LOI had been opened prior to March 31, 2000. Further they have stated that the matter is
sub judice.

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that while rationalizing the duty structure compatible with WTO guidelines, the Government should protect the
interests of the domestic paper industries.
        The Committee views the Government’s Policy of reducing customs duty from 35% to 30% as against the WTO bound rate of 40% as a major
threat for the domestic paper industries. The Committee conceives that the reduction in customs duty would definitely encourage import, which in
turn, would adversely affect the paper industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should review its decision and revise
the custom duty to 35% or 40%.

industries. The Committee also recommends that the BHI should take up this subject with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) for
reversing the custom duty on newsprint from the present 5% to 20% which is still lower to the WTO bond rate of 25%.

ad-valorem.

Dear Shri Yashwant Sinhaji,
        As you are aware the capital goods industry is witnessing an unprecedented demand recession, causing declining market prices and erosion in
domestic market share. Capital goods sector has witnessed a decline of 2.7% in April-Sept.2000 as compared to a growth of 5% in 1999-2000 and
11% in 1998-99.
2.     Some of the factors responsible for deceleration are slow down in investment, reduction in the custom duty on capital goods/project imports
from a high of 85% to 0-5%. Domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, high cost of finance and

101st report of Committee on Industry

infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports.
3.     This situation is further aggravated by the issue of notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99 which allows import of goods for the projects financed by
the United Nations, World Bank, Asian Development Bank and other International organizations at “Nil” duty. Due to this notification, domestic
manufacturers are not able to avail the price preference of 15% for projects funded by such agencies.
4.     You are aware that the capital goods sector has very strong backward and forward linkages. Therefore, it is necessary to provide support to give
the desired impetus to this industry for reversing the declining trend and sustain its growth. In this context, I have following suggestions for your
consideration -----
        l     Custom Duty on all capital goods should be brought to bound rate of WTO.
        l     In project imports, restructure this present duty structure by levying minimum basic custom duty of 15% + CVD equal to excise duty @ 8%
or lower and rescind notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99.
        l     Restoration of Terminal Excise Duty (TED) to domestic suppliers to projects where the end product is not exciseable.
        With regards,

CHAPTER–I
MEMORANDUM  OF  UNDERSTANDING  BETWEEN  FERTILIZER  PSUS  AND DEPARTMENT  OF 
FERTILIZERS
1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU
System. The targets are finalised at the beginning of the year and so are the commitments of the Department of
Fertilizers. The evaluation of the performance of these targets is carried out only at the end of the year. The focus under
the MoU system hence is said to have shifted from mere input orientation to result orientation. This also envisages a
system granting more autonomy to the PSUs with lesser involvement of the Ministries and Departments in the control of
the day-to-day functioning of the PSUs through laid down procedures etc.

2.1       MFL was incorporated in December, 1966 as a public sector undertaking with authorised share capital of Rs. 14
crores in December, 1966 with Government of India and AMOCO India Inc. (a wholly owned subsidiary of Standard
Oil Company of USA) holding 51% and 49% shares respectively. MFL commenced commercial production in
November, 1971. Subsequently, in 1972 as per the Formation Agreement, National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC - a
multi billion state-owned petro-chemical company of Iran) was inducted as shareholder acquiring 50% of AMOCO
shareholding in MFL.
2.2       In 1985, AMOCO, pursuant to their worldwide strategy, disinvested their shares, which were in turn acquired by
Government of India and NIOC. The current shareholding pattern is as follows :

            Public                                                                           15.82%
            The paid-up equity capital of the company as on 31.3.2000 is Rs. 162.05 crores.
2.3       MFL is engaged in the manufacture of Ammonia, Urea, complex fertilizers and bio-fertilizers. MFL's activities
include marketing of these fertilizers and trading in Agro-chemicals in accordance with the corporate objective. MFL
has its plant facilities and head quarters located on a sprawling 350 acres at Manali, about 20 kms. north of Chennai

considering the long-term benefits for the company and to overcome the present problems of port congestion and port-
to-plant logistics.
2.5       In this backdrop, MFL is planning to set up a Captive Fertilizer Berth as a joint venture project to handle 2
million TPA of Dry bulk and Liquid cargo, made up of 1.5 million MT is dry bulk cargo comprising of Urea, MOP,
DAP and finished grades of fertilizer and 0.5 MT liquid cargo comprising of Phosphoric acid and Liquid ammonia.
Modern handling facilities like Unloading Systems, Bagging Systems and Transit Storage form part of the project.
2.6       MFL is in the process of engaging a consultant to select a suitable Joint Venture Partner, among 12 parties who
have evinced interest to participate in this Captive Fertilizer Berth Project.
CAPTIVE  POWER
2.7       MFL consumes around 130 million unit of electrical power per year drawn from TNEB grid and also from
captive generation. 8 Diesel Generators and 2 Gas Turbines generate 32.7 million units (25%) per year as captive power.
2.8       To tide over frequent power failure, under-frequency and voltage fluctuations of TNEB grid, MFL is seeking
alternate power capacity from outside supply sources other than TNEB.
2.9       MFL had preliminary discussion with Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) for participation in their
proposed Rs. 2837 crore Independent Power Plant (IPP) Project of 500 MW capacity.
2.10     In the meantime, MFL is holding negotiation with CPCL for wheeling 4 to 5 MW of surplus power from their
existing captive Power Plant facility.
2.11     The company did not pay dividend to its shareholders after 1992-93. It is running in losses. The loss was
contributed by shortfall in production of urea and NPK, reduction in contribution for NPK, higher specific consumption
of raw materials, steep exchange rate variation, monsoon failure resulting in lower sales, higher rebates and discounts
and higher interest cost.
2.12     The company's operations continue to be unprofitable. During April and May 2001, Ammonia plant load had to
be restricted due to high Ammonia inventory levels caused by poor off-take by downstream urea/NPL plants. Similarly,
urea plant was also operated at low levels as off-take of NPK for sale has been poor. The annual turnaround was taken
up on May 28, 2001 with a schedule to complete it on June 22, 2001. However, due to the unexpected developments,
the turnaround was extended and the company could come back to production stream in respect of NH
3 only on August
3, 2001. Keeping in view the advice given by urea reactor manufacturers, the company decided to get the urea reactor
inspected which was not envisaged in the original schedule. The inspection of reactor was a difficult job involving
erection of structure above the reactor with hoisting facility. Though an attempt was made to erect the structure while
the plant was in operation, enough progress could not be made due to unfavourable environmental conditions. After the
shut down of the plants, erection work was taken up and hoists were provided at the top level of about 60 mtrs. height to
life the reactor bundles, each weighing 36 T. Reactor B was inspected on July 18 and after attending to some minor
repairs was boxed up.
2.13     In contrast, the inspection of reactor 'A' revealed extensive damages. A quick assessment was made and
necessary action was initiated by the company to rectify the bundles. Notwithstanding all these constraints, the company
decided to start and run the Ammonia and Urea plants at around 50% load. The quality of Urea being produced now is
relatively better with temperature of the Prill hovering around 50
o Celsius, which are the main objectives of Urea Prill
Tower modifications, aimed and achieved by the company. The repair works to Reactor 'A' involve procurement of
imported materials, extensive welding and other specialized jobs, which has been entrusted on a turnkey basis to the
manufacturer M/s Nooter Fabricators Inc. USA to secure Guarantee Test Run of urea plant.

2.15     MFL has submitted original FACR proposal to Government of India during January 1999. Whereas the proposal
relating to FIs have been approved and implemented by them during April 1999, the proposal submitted to Government
of India has undergone several revisions till date. In view of the losses incurred during 2000-01 and continuing during
the current year 2001-02 MFL has requested for a revised FACR packages from Government of India and other
institutions, which have extended long term/short term assistance. In respect of FIs, the revised proposal inter-alia
included downward revision of interest rate with moratorium on principal and interest payment for 2 years. With regard
to Government of India loans, the proposal provides for waiver of interest amounting to Rs. 71 crores and downward
reduction of interest rate. Similarly, the revised FACR envisages lower interest on the working capital assistance
received from commercial banks. With a view to avoid company becoming sick, the FIs and Government of India are
working out a comprehensive package.

the company has been operating with costly feedstock like Naphtha on one hand and high capital-related charged on the

order to reduce the yawning gap between cost of production and realization, company has represented to Tariff
Commission to reckon industry related/MFL specific problems in the areas of :-

2.       At the outset the Chairman welcomed the Members and apprised them of agenda for the meeting of the day.
3.       The Committee thereafter, took up Auto Policy for discussion. The Chairman apprised the Members that the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry had recommended in its 59th Report that the Government should
formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its Action Taken Note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1     The Chairman stated that the Committee on Industry took up the Auto Policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.
3.2.    The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in
this regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24th June and 16th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on
24th June, 2002 a questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In
the meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI); Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA)
and Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of fuel saver). Apprising
the Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in
Auto Policy which inter-alia  included import of second hand imported cars; lack of testing facilities; foreign direct

3.3     The Committee, thereafter, discussed in details the aims of Auto Policy which aimed at to promote integrated,
phased, enduring and self-sustained growth of the Indian Automobile Industry. The Committee discussed also the
objective of Auto Policy which inter-alia include promotion of a globally competitive automotive industry; exalting the
sector as a lever of industrial growth and an employment; establishment of an international hub for manufacturing small
affordable passenger cars and key centre for manufacturing tractors and two wheelers in the world; ensuing a balanced
transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian economy and local industry; modernisation of the industry by
facilitating indigenous design, research and development; steering up India's software industry into automotive
technology; development of domestic safety and environmental standard at par with international standards; assisting
development of vehicles propelled by alternative energy sources.

            The Committee is happy to note the savings on the specified overheads due to measures undertaken by HSCL

            The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package as proposed by the Ministry of
Steel and so approved by the Government was not as comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total
liability of HSCL.  The Company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in general because
implementation of the revival package would respond only if approved measures are taken in time for total and
comprehensive restructuring of the Company.  HSCL needs total overhauling and complete and comprehensive
restructuring in one go as partial package and delayed implementation defeats the whole idea, approach and action.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the Financial Restructuring Package, granted by Government of India during July, 99, a proposal
for further revival of the Company was submitted in June, 01 to the Finance Ministry by Ministry of Steel.

Recommendation ( Para 7.3)
 
System of Sub-Contracting Business Pattern
           
            The Committee understands the compelling circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of sub-
contracting business pattern but it is also an open secret that sub-contracting gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the Company itself.  The Committee is of the view that VRS offer by HSCL to its employees would take
care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of productive age profile and willing to undertake work/assignment
from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give
larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of
sub-contracting is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees, sooner than later.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the separation of manpower in accordance with the provision of the Restructuring Proposal and
MOU with Ministry of Steel,  HSCL will be left out with only about 1000 employees on its rolls.  In such
circumstances, HSCL’s function will  be of supervisory nature only.  However, execution of contracts will be carried
out as per the approved procedures of the Company.  Adequate steps will be taken to optimize margins and use of
departmental inputs.
 
Further recommendation
 
            The Committee feels that  entrusting  HSCL merely  with the supervisory role  and continuing  with   the system
of sub-contracting would not be  a  sustainable proposition  for the Company.   There is no need   for making a mini
Ministry   with in the  Ministry  of Steel .  The Ministry of Steel is already playing the  supervisory role  over the steel
PSUs,   therefore,  steel PSUs should  do the actual  work, the Committee feels .  The Committee,  therefore,   reiterates  
that   direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give  larger  margin to HSCL and thus opening  scope for
profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of sub-contracting is  replaced  by direct involvement
of HSCL employees, sooner than later.

The Committee is of the view that  HSCL management , while making  settlement  of full and final   accounts
for all HSCL employees who have opted for VRS,  should  differentiate the cases of pending settlement due to audit
objection and arrears to be settled on account of outstanding wages and salaries for these  employees due to  lack of 
financial resources on the part of  the Company.  The HSCL management and the Ministry of Steel  should  expedite  
the process of making settlement  of outstanding  wages and salaries  with the sanction of the    revival package.   The
Committee further recommends that  as soon as  the legal  wrangles    regarding   the implementation  of the 
recommendation   of the Fifth Pay Commission  gets  solved  and  the Ministry of Finance    releases  financial
assistance to HSCL ,    balance dues  of the retired /separated employees should be made .
 
Recommendation ( Para 16.3 )
 
Non-plan assistance of Rs.125.17 crore
 
            The Committee however, is of the view that the Ministry of Finance should consider the proposal of the Ministry
of Steel for grant of non-plan assistance of   Rs.125.17 crore to enable HSCL to discharge its liabilities towards payment
of arrears of wages and salaries of its employees.  The Committee is of the opinion that once a comprehensive package
for revival of HSCL is sanctioned in one go the Company would be able to come out of red.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Ministry of Steel has been pursuing the matter relating to grant of full financial assistance to the Company
to enable it to discharge its entire liability towards payment of wages and salaries to its employees.  As mentioned

            The Committee notes that the reasons as placed by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of HSCL.  The

sudden increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further opines that HSCL’s present suffering is due to error of
judgment and some elements were beyond the control of management and Government due to prevailing circumstances,
lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes of HSCL.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Mines (Ministry of Coal and
Mines) on the Recommendations contained in the  64
th  Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry) on  Modernisation, Restructuring  and Expansion Programme of Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL) 
and  post disinvestment performance of  Hindustan  Zinc Ltd in the background of the shareholders agreement.  
Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL),  one of the leading producers of lead and zinc, was incorporated   in January 1968 as a
public sector Company after the take over of the erstwhile Metal Corporation of India Limited, to develop mining and
smelting capacities to meet the domestic demand of zinc and lead metals..   The authotrised share capital of HZL is Rs.
500 crore and the paid up capital is Rs. 422.53 crore.  The Government held 75.92% of the equity as 24.08% of its
equity was disinvested during the period 1991-93.  Government decided to further disinvest 26% equity capital of HZL
to a strategic partner with an appropriate role in management. On 11
th April,,2002, the Government has disinvested 26%
equity of HZL and management of the company wastransferred to the Strategic Partner  (S.P.) namely, M/s Sterlite
Opportunities and Ventures Ltd. with this  disinvestment the stake  of the Government in the Company has come
down    to 49.92% . Sub-Committee   on Ministry of Mines and Coal under the  convertion of Shri A.C Jose  (LS)

disinvestment  the stake of Government in  the company had come down to  49.92%  which was less than 50% and
hence HZL was no longer a Public Sector Undertaking.  Therefore, it may not be advisable to furnish an Action Taken
Note (ATN) on 64th Report. 
 
3.            However,  the argument of the Department of Mines  was found untenable   and therefore was found not
justifiable on the following grounds:-
1.      64th  Report  was presented to the parliament on the 8 th march, 2002 and forwarded to the Department of
Mines for furnishing action taken note prior to disinvestment of Hindustan Zinc Ltd.
2.      Even after disinvestment the Government stake continued to be to the tune of 49.92% which indicated
Government's substantial stake in the company
3.      Recommendations contained in the 64th Report also covered the disinvestment aspect whereupon the
Department of Mines should have given the detailed information for the Members of the Committee.
4.      The Department of Mines should have furnished the details regarding 'share purchase agreements ", details
of understandings reached between the Government and M/s Sterlite Opportunities and Ventures Ltd. , mode
of management etc. in the post divested phase,
5.
      The Government's representatives would be the Members of, Board of Directors' who would participate in
the meeting of the Board and act as a link between the new management of the company in post divested
phase and the Government, therefore, such the representatives of Government would ultimately supervise the
functioning of the company and therefore the company would remain in fact under the overall supervision of
the Government. Therefore, it was reasonable that Government/Departments should continue to furnish
information to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee whenever it is sought .
 
6.
      The Hindustan Zinc Ltd. even in the past divested era would continue to utilize the national resources and
therefore should continue to be responsible and responsive to the nation/Government and people of the
country in general.
 
7.      The purpose of disinvestment was although to generate revenue, but most importantly to inject operational
efficiency and managerial effectiveness in the company and for the general benefit of the economy.  The
purpose was not doing away of accountability in the system.
 
8.      In order to avoid the repetition of what happened to VSNL and TATA  quagmire over a decision regarding
investment, it is suggested the companies management should continue to be responsible to the Government
to post divested phase and on this count should continue to furnish information to Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee as and when asked for.

PRODUCTION CAPACITY OF HINDUSTAN ZINC LTD.
The Committee notes the Ore  production  capacity of    Hindustan Zinc Ltd. Mines  and recommends that HZL
management should make efforts  for  optimisation of production   to the maximum extent    at the  commercial level  
and  operation of each mines  with the minimum of  waste .  The efforts may be made for   reduction in the   cost of 
operating   Mines by employing   latest tools and technology.     The capacity utilisation of Jawar Mines,   Rajpura
Dariba    Sargipalli have been quite low . Steps may be taken to improve the same.
(Para 4.3)
The Committee appreciates the HZL management in general and employees of Debari Zinc Smelter and Vizag 
Electrolytic  Zinc Smelter for  commendable capacity utilisation .  The Committee feels that   while  there is a scope for
improving  capacity  utilisation at Vizag plant , and the at the same time the Committee recommends that efforts should
be made for  maximizing the capacity  utilisation of all   HZL smelter  since the   measures undertaken would reduce the
cost of production.
(Para 4.5)

 The Committee was informed that Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL) was disinvested on11.4.2002.  A shareholders
agreement (SHA) has been signed between the Government of India and M/s Sterlite Opportunities and Ventures
Limited (SOVL), who are the Strategic Partners (SP).The SHA  stipulates the terms and conditions for managing the
affairs of disinvested HZL including reconstitution of the Board of Directors. In terms of this Agreement the SP has
the right to nominate six directors who will be called “Purchaser Nominee Director” including “Managing Director”
of the company. The Government shall have the right to nominate five directors and will be called “Government
Nominee Director” and all will be non-executive directors of the company. The Chairperson of the Board of
disinvested HZL would be from the Government Nominee Directors till such time as the SP holds less than 51 per
cent of the share capital.
 
  2.       The Board of the Company is expected to manage the affairs of the company in accordance with the Articles of
Association of the Company and Companies Act 1956. For smooth transaction of the business of the company the
Articles of Association of HZL as PSU requiring amendment were identified and now have been amended in extra-
ordinary general meeting of the company.  Despite this, Schedule 4.5 of SHA identifies the matters for which special
consent is required from the Government for transacting the business envisaged in those items. A few examples
requiring affirmative note from Government are as follows:

            Winding up the Company voluntarily.

INTRODUCTION 
         I, the Chairman of  the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having 
been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Sixth Report on the Globalisation 
and capital goods industry pertaining to the Department of Public En terprises, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. 
2.      The Committee, in this context, held m eetings with various Minist ries and representatives o f
Industry Organisations on 16 th April, 8 th May, 25 th June, 12 th August and 27 th November, 2002 
respectively. 
3.      The Committee in its meeting held on 17th December, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
 
  
CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTION 
         A new trend of global integration began to emerge all over the world in 1980s. This was facilitated
by the gradual integration of the world economics, which ensured free flow of capital and goods from
one country to another country. Foreign capital is now freely available to finance the large infrastructure
projects. Acceptance of WTO regime  by most of the countries has si nce led to a gradual abolition o f
quantitative restrictions and reduction duties and removal of restrictions on inter-country trade. 
1.1    In our context, the Industr ial Policy of 1991 starte d the process of de-lic ensing and except 18 
industries, licensing was withdrawn. The process of de-regul ation was aimed at en larging competition 
and allowing new firms to enter the market s. The market was opened up to domestic
entrepreneurs/industrialists, which as reserved for public sector unde rtakings, and foreign capital was
provided free entry up to 51% equity in high technol ogy areas. With the adve nt of globalization, when
World Bank-aided projects started to come to country, the lifting of import control and drastic reduction 
of import duties, competition from overseas posed a proble m to the domestic capital goods industry. It
has become difficult to stay in the race for this industry in the fa ce of stiff competition from the
multinational giants. 
1.2    Despite the tremendous odds even on date, there are examples of various domestic Indian
companies in sectors like automobi les, steel, engineering, etc. in both public and private sectors that
have successfully with stood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian economy; fo r
example Maruti cars are being exported and Tata have similar plans. TISCO has been recognized as one
of the least cost steel producers in the world and companies like IRCON, BHEL and L&T have been
successfully executing contracts abroad. These com panies have mana ged to meet the stiff com petition

from foreign giants but the ab sence of a level playing field put increasing pressures on thei r
competitiveness and profitability. 
1.3    The Committee deliberated upon the matter and in its 36th Report observed as under:
 
         “One such company (BHEL) which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by 
the liberalization of Indian econom y. The impressive track record of  it calls for a special mention 
of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy 
Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race  despite the odds faced by  it as a result of stif f 
competition unleashed by the multina tional giants operating in its fi eld of specialization namely, 
manufacture of power plants. T hough BHEL has managed to sustain it s viability yet it is facing 
some unfair challenges. The abse nce of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational competitors 
has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This  is leading to an eve r-increasing pressure on 
its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly  upgrading its technology and has 
also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC  power projects. This 
reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve th e nation even when the odds are 
stacked against it. Therefor e, what this company requires is a li ttle help from th e Government in 
the form of suitable policy measures. In this re gard, the sub-committee draw s the attention of the 
Government to the issues of pr ice and purchase preference to BHEL, and import duty concessions 
to the foreign companies. Through  in some cases price and purchas e preference is granted to the 
PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to 
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exempti ons are precisely the 
reasons for the playing field not be ing level for domestic companies or  for that matter PSUs as the 
bids offered by foreign players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other 
words, the competition is killed well before it begins. The Committee believes that the need of the 
hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide  a level playing field to all the 
players for the sake of healthy competition. 
Committee’s Recommendations 
1.3.1   In view of the above, the Committee has come to the conclusion that the Government should take
necessary policy measures to extend 15% price and purchase preference to BHEL  
vis-à-vis its bids for domestic power projects. It also recommends that the Government should review its
policy of giving duty concessions to the foreign companies in as much as it leads to disadvantages to the
domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered view  of the committee that foreign
companies should not be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.” 
Comments from Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises are as under: 
       “The Ministry has taken up the following issues with the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of 
Commerce: 
1.    Restoration of refund of terminal excise duty as  available to domestic bidders in the Exim
Policy 1999-2000. 
2.    Continuance of the Price Preference of 15% to domestic bidders in case of World Bank/ADB
funded projects irrespective of the rate of customs duty. 
Alternatively….... 
Equipment imports in the case of project s funded by UN/World Bank/ADB should attract
customs duty of at least 15%. 
1.3.2   Ministry of Commerce declined the proposal of this ministry to restore refund of Terminal Excise
Duty (TED) in EXIM Policy 1999-2000, as these bene fits are directly rela ted to the incidence o f
Customs Duty (CD) and C ounter Veiling Duty (CVD) on the imports for the project, i.e. whenever the
imports are exempted from the incidence of CVD, the domestic supplier is given the benefit of refund of
TED. In the budget 2000-2001, in respect of power projects other than mega-power projects, fertilizer 
projects and refineries, CVD has been  increased to 16% and therefore the benefits of refund of TED is
withdrawn from such projects.

1.3.3   A meeting was held by the Finance Secretary on 26.7.2000 to discuss the issue regarding the
competitiveness of domestic industries. As a follow up of this meeting, a note highlighting the following
three issues which are adversely affecting the dom estic industries was circul ated to the concerned
Ministries/Departments by the Department of Revenue: 
           (i)   Restoration of refund of TED in EXIM Policy 2000-01. 
           (ii)   Applicability of withdrawal of refund of TED for contracts finalized before 31.03.2000. 
           (iii)  Rescindment for Custom s Notification No. 85/99-CUS dated 06.07.1999 permitting imports 
at zero duty by projects funded by International organizations. 
1.3.4   After analyzing the view expressed by th e various concerned Depa rtments, Department o f
Revenue summarized the position and recommended to this Ministry to take up the issue with TRU and

1.3.5   Accordingly, the issue rega rding restoration of TED for cont racts finalized before 31.3.2000 was

           The other issues mentioned in Sl. No. (i) and (iii) above have been taken up with the TRU. This is

1.4      The Committee again considered the matter and in its 45th Report and  observed as under:
 
           The Committee now recommends that the Ministry of Finance sh ould take early decision in
respect of rescindment of Custom Notificati on No. 85/9/CUS dated 6.7.1999, which allows import at
zero duty and DGFT should consider, as  special case, to issue notificat ion for refund of terminal excise

1.4.1   The Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises has replied as under: 
           “Ministry of Finance, Department of  Revenue has been apprised of the observations of the 
Committee that they should take ear ly decision in respect of resci ndment of Custom Notification No.
85/9/CUS dated 6.7.1999 which allows import at zer o duty in respect of Wo rld Bank funded projects
and have been requested to convey its decision to this Department. 
14.2    Further, DGFT have been apprised of th e observations of the Com mittee that they should
consider, as a special case , to issue notification for refund of Terminal Excise  Duty (TED) for purchase
order/bids under international competitive bidding prior to 1.4.2000  and have been requested to
reconsider the issue and convey their decision to this Department. 
14.3    After re-examination of th e matter, DGFT have now sent th eir response in which they have
reiterated the stand taken by them earlier. They have stated that the issue regarding withdrawal of refund
of Terminal Excise Duty is li nked to the increase in the CVD to 16% a nnounced in the budged in
February 2000. As any import, which would have taken place after 1.4.2000 would have been subject to
the imposition of CVD, all the supplies affected from this date will not be entitled to refund of TED. 
14.4    Further, on this issue, DGFT are contesting a cour t case against M/S Ma lana Power Company in

CHAPTER – III 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
3.        The amendment of Customs Notification N o. 85/99 dated 6.7.1999 was issued amending the 
earlier Notification No. 84/99 permitting imports at zero duty for projects funded by international
Organizations. With th e notification, the preference polic y under World Ba nk guideline has
automatically reduced to zero and adversely affected the domestic industry. The Committee consistently
followed up the matter and recommende d for corrective measures in its 36 th, 45th and 59th Reports and 
had five meetings with several mi nistries and public and private sect or domestic industry to resolve the
matter. The World Bank issue is not only applicable  to Public Sector Undert akings but also to capital
goods industry in general. The Committee’s objective was to utilize it for the development of the
country. 
3.1      The Committee recalls that in the meetings held on 16 th April, 8th May and 25th June, 2002, The 
Ministries/Departments had expresse d their own reservations and concer ns but ultimately they realized
that if only they put their heads together they could resolve the i ssue. The Committee appreciates the
ministries and departments for their coordinated approach. 
3.2      Since globalization, the country is facing ma ny problems but at the sa me time the country cannot
go back. We have to see how to safeguard the country’s interest – both public and private sectors. 
3.3      Now, in view of the clarificatory notification issued by the Department of  Economic Affairs,
there is no need to rescind the Notification No. 85/99 and the Comm ittee hopes that the capital goods
industry of the country would be ab le to compete with the foreign bi dders in the projects funded by
international organizations. The Committee, however, urges upon the i ndustry to keep vigil and watch
with regard to any deviation of the World Bank gui deline by any international agency by not including
the price preference clause in the NIT (Notice I nviting Tender) and thereby depriving the domestic
industry to bid for the project and the industry should also immediately bring any instance to the notice
of Department of Economic Affairs in case such price preference is not extended to domestic industry
by any multinational organizations. 
3.4      The Committee understands more internati onal funded projects would come to the country in
future and the domestic industry w ould be able to reap the benefi t and contribute to the country’s 
development.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between stipulated
delivery period and the actual date of delivery.
3.         As per standard terms of conditions of supply contract generally also provide for force majeure clause meaning
unforeseen circumstances like legal injunctions, natural calamities, industrial action by workers etc. are reasons
attributable to the delay in supply or performance, the same is exempt from imposition of liquidated damages.
4.         The Sub-Committee-III for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises of Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry came to know about the effect of Liquidated Damages on the supplier
when it visited Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels at Visakhapatnam (a subsidiary of BYNL) on 11th July, 2000. The
workers union as well as management of BHPV informed the Committee that due to delay in deliveries, Rs. 41 crores
had been held up with different units of the company which had created cash flow problems. Later on, after visiting

held on 9th November, 2000. The Convenor, after hearing the Secretaries, Department of Heavy Industry, and Ministry
of Petroleum and Natural Gas, about the present status of the outstanding issues of amounts of BYNL group of
companies withheld by various oil sector PSUS on account of LD and other disputed matters, directed the Secretary,

Natural Gas for advising the Oil PSUs to consider these cases favourably. The Committee also directed to follow it up
by personal visits by representatives of BYNL and their respective subsidiaries to the concerned Oil PSUs.
5.         Thereafter,  the Committee on Industry in its 44th Report present/laid on 21st December, 2000 recommended as
follows :
5.1       The Committee also came to know during its interaction with the workers and management of some PSUs that
due to non-delivery of final goods in schedule time, penalties have been imposed on them in the form of Liquidity
Damages (LD) which are proving a death knell for some of them.
5.2       The Department of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with the client PSUs for release of outstanding
amount locked-up on account of Liquidity Damages (LD) to such a possible extent, which can be released by the client
PSUs. This will be a helpful gesture to the PSUs who are having working capitalproblem.
5.3       The Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprise in their Action Taken Note informed that Government had
been taking up the matter with the concerned Ministries/Departments for release of withheld amount on account of LDs.
6.         This was reported to the House vide Committee's 60th report presented/laid on the 19th December, 2001. Since
the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industry could not bear much fruit, 
Sub-Committee-III observed that these issues needed to be approached through a coordinated effort. The Committee
also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns expressed by DHI in respect of the said issue by the other
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, decided to hear both the Department of Heavy Industry and the Ministry of
Petroleum and Natural Gas to find out a probable solution.
CHAPTER–II
MEETINGS HELD WITH THE MINISTRIES AND PSUS THEREUNDER
7.         The Committee held meetings on 17th April, 13th August and 4th December, 2002 on the issue. The
deliberations of the Committee are given below :
Meeting held on 17th April, 2002
7.1       At the outset, the Convenor welcomed the Secretaries of the Ministries of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises and Petroleum and Natural Gas, and representatives of various Central PSUs. The Convenor apprised the
Committee that the Committee had been pursuing the case of liquidated damages, which had been imposed by the client
PSUs on the supplier PSUs for non-adherence to the delivery schedule. There had been some problems among the
PSUs. These Liduidated Damages were imposed due to delay and as a result the money had been held up and the
supplier PSUs, specially the BYNL group of companies, had been facing working capital problem.
7.2       Secretary,  Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that the engineering
industries were facing some problems as there had been no fresh investment in the economy. One of the main problems
had been the lack of working capital because the working capital limits had become irregular. The banks were not
willing to give further advance and the Government was also reluctant to issue fresh funds for the working capital. The
BYNL group of companies had a large measure of support from oil sector and the oil sector was one sector in the
economy where there had been some investment. About 50% of the turnover of these companies came from the oil
PSUs and generally oil sector PSUs also gave benefit of purchase preference to these companies. There had been delay
in execution of projects but in the recent past, these companies had assured that things had improved and some of those
delays or level of delays or the extent of delays that took place earlier, were not taking place now. The process of
disinvestments in all these companies was under way and in order to optimise the return to the Government, the

107th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/107threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:24:58]
Ministry was trying to do everything that would add value to these companies and if these companies were running well
or better, the chances were that it would get Expression of Interest and also a better price. He further informed that in
some of the major cases wherever there were some delays, the delays were sometimes due to involvement of various
parties or changes in specifications. But he had been assured that delay on the part of BYNL group of companies did not
contribute to the additional delay. He requested that in such cases at least the Boards of oil PSUs could take lenient
view. If some of the major cases could be disposed of in such a way, the working capital problem could be solved and
most other problems could be taken care of.
7.3       Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum, informed that on the recommendation of the Committee, the agreement
between Department of Heavy Industries and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas for placing of orders on these
companies, which expired on January, 2002, had been extended upto 2003. As far as liquidated damages were
concerned, the Ministry had written to the companies to take up the matter with the Boards.
7.4       He further stated that some progress had been made, but it was slow. He requested the Committee that if the
Department of Heavy Industries considered this issue as an issue applicable to all PSUs across the board and issue
policy guidelines, it would be much easier for them to take action in the matter. He further informed that all the
guidelines which were given and which were under contemplation of the Department of Programme Implementation
envisaged that liquidated damages may be imposed upto a certain value. That was their real problem. However, BYNL
group of companies could now bid without any bank guarantee. They did not require Original Manufacturer's
Certification and oil PSUs would continue to give them existing purchase preference.
7.5       The Convenor at that point said that BYNL group of companies should improve their delivery schedule as a
small delay on their part resulted in a great loss for the oil PSUs.
7.5.1    Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas, thereupon, suggested that Liquidated Damages upto March, 2001 should
be taken up for discussion to see how they could be settled. Thereupon, the Convenor requested both the Secretaries to
prepare a joint report on the subject for consideration of the Committee. The Sub-Committee strongly recommended
that all liquidated damages, as outstanding on 31.3.2001 should be resolved through this joint exercise, which was
agreed upon by both the Secretaries.
7.6       On the basis of the discussion held on 17th April, the Committee on Industry in its 72nd report observed that :
7.6.1    The Sub-Committee-III had a meeting with the Ministries of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and
Petroleum and Natural Gas where the question of Liquidity Damages (LD) came up. The Liquidity Damages is a form
of penalty, which is imposed by the client PSEs on the supplier PSEs for non-adhering to schedule delivery within the
stipulated time. Since BYNL consists of small companies, the imposition of this penalty proved a setback for these
companies. The Secretary, DHI, stated, "the reason for delay in supplying items was due to the shortage of working
capital. If suitable advances are given to the supplier PSEs then this problem can be sorted out". He further suggested,
"The Liquidity Damages pertaining to the last millennium should be waived". The Sub-Committee agreed with the
proposal.
7.7       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should assist the companies wherever and
whenever the companies under the DHI are facing working capital problem and are not able to execute the orders in
hand. The Government should assist the companies under the DHI to meet the shortage of working capital in the form of
Bank Guarantee, non-plan loans, etc. The Committee further recommends that the DHI should help these companies by
getting advances from the client PSEs for the execution of the work orders. The Committee also suggests that under One
Time Settlement, all the cases of Liquidity Damages upto March, 2001 may be considered and settled. The Committee
recommends that both the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and the Ministry of Petroleum and
Natural Gas should make joint efforts to resolve the issue relating to the Liquidity Damages for placement of work
orders on the BYNL group of companies.
7.8       The Department of Heavy Industries in their Action Taken Note informed that :
            As far as the issue of release of withheld payments by the oil PSUs on account of LDs, it is stated that this issue
has also been raised in the 44th report on the Parliamentary Standing Committee as well as in the oral evidence held on
17.4.2002 before the Parliamentary Standing Committee. The Committee has already been informed about the efforts
being made by the Department of Heavy Industries to resolve the issue. However, the Parliamentary Standing

Committee during the oral evidence meeting held on 17.4.2002 has suggested that the Secretaries of the Department of
Heavy Industries and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas should prepare a joint report on the subject for
consideration of the Committee so that the issue of all the LDs (as on 31.3.2001) should be resolved through this joint
exercise. A joint meeting between the two ministries to resolve the issue was held on 8th August 2002. The Committee
was apprised of the outcome of the exercise in the meeting held on 13.8.2002.
8.         Meeting held on 13th August 2002
8.1       The Convenor welcomed the Members of the Sub-Committee and the representatives of Ministries of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises and Petroleum and Natural Gas and also representatives of the ONGC, HPCL, IOCL,
GAIL, OIL and BPCL.
8.2       The Convenor apprised the Sub-Committee that at its last meeting held on the 17th April, 2002 the issue relating
to liquidated damages imposed on the Bharat Yantra Nigam Ltd. (BYNL) Group of Companies by the Oil Companies
came up for discussion and the Committee opined that liquidated damages upto March, 2002 should be settled.
However, Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas suggested that Liquidated Damages upto March, 2001 would be taken
up as a special case and after having interaction with the various Oil Boards, a solution would be found.
8.3       Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas informed the Committee that the matter was discussed with
the various Boards of the oil companies and the following proposals had been mooted for consideration :–
8.3.1    Whichever future project would be taken up by BYNL Group of Companies, 50% of the project cost would be
paid to them in advance as soft loan. BYNL would put forth remaining 50% to complete the project.
8.3.2    As stated by the BYNL, there had been an element of contributory negligence on the part of organizations also.
The details of the contributory negligence may be given to Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas for onward
transmission to the respective Boards for review.
8.3.3    The cases where losses occurred due to delay in supply of equipment were to be seen separately.
8.3.4    The cases where supply of equipment did not result in any delay in completion of projects would be considered
sympathetically.
8.4       The Secretary added that this was a broad approach and as asked by Department of Heavy Industries, one time
dispensation or half-a-time dispensation might not be possible.
8.5       Department of Heavy Industries informed the Committee that Department of Heavy Industries agreed with all
points made by Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas except that there was one major point of disagreement.
Department of Heavy Industries suggested that an ad hoc amount of 50 per cent be released from the Liquidated
Damages and that would augment the ways and means position of BYNL companies and Department of Heavy
Industries would give some kind of guarantee on that amount. Rest of the amounts can be settled as and when a view
was taken by the respective Boards. The second point the Department of Heavy Industry made was on capacity building
keeping in view the country was opening up and it would have a different kind of import regime. Companies would be
coming to Petroleum and construction sector and user sector and capital goods sector should help each other in building
a certain capacity to reap benefit of the new situation.
8.6       After hearing both the Ministers, the Convenor observed that both the Secretaries should meet and sort out the
matter. He stressed that it was one time help that was being sought. He desired that Ministry of Petroleum & Natural
Gas and Department of Heavy Industries should come out with certain suggestions before the Committee for its
consideration within ten days.
8.7       The Committee also expressed its satisfaction as the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas agreed to pay Rs. 20
crores as advance to Bharat Heavy Plate and Vessels (BHPV) for completing the projects in Assam and Bihar.
9.         Meeting held on 4th December, 2002
9.1       The Convenor welcomed the Secretaries of the Ministries of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises, and
Petroleum and Natural Gas and representatives of the PSUs thereunder. The Convenor recalled that in the last meeting
both the Secretaries were directed to consider the matter relating to LD. He wanted to know the present status.

9.2       Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry, informed that they had promised that they would try to liquidate the
LDs etc. Over a period of time information had been supplied to the Committee that about 3 crores have already been
liquidated. Rs. 62 crores was still pending and one of the reasons for pendency was that the petroleum companies as
well as their companies were not able to reconcile the figures. That did not indicate a very good health of negotiations.
Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas informed that (1) there were problem on both sides. In a number of
cases there had been delays by the companies for supplying equipments. In some cases ONGC were at fault because of
which they had difficulty in supplying. It had been decided that he and Secretary, Heavy Industry would meet once a
month to consider these questions of coordination. (2) As far as the question of liquidated damages was concerned, it
had been decided that they would give an opportunity to BYNL companies to make a presentation before the Board of
these oil companies where they would give an entire point of view and then the Board would take a view.
            Representatives of IOC informed that they had teamed up with BYNL. Two projects were in motion—one at
Barauni and other at Digboi — and these would be completed soon. CMD, GAIL, informed that they had been in touch
with BYNL. There were issues of reconciliation because BYNL's records and their records were not tallying. The first
exercise would be that they had a mutually agreed number of what had been recovered. CMD, ONGC, informed that
there had been slippages in the matter of supplying and commissioning equipments. From April this year, they had
reduced their gas flaring by 35% in Gandhar. If they get additional compressors from BYNL, they would be able to
reduce it to 80% in the current financial year.
9.3       The Convenor observed that ONGC's loss was country's loss. He asked the BYNL to state what had gone wrong.
CMD, BYNL, informed that after the LC was opened the main bottleneck had been the imported engines. They had
promised 10th November and 15th December for 6th and 7th compressor. 6th was despatched on 30th November and
7th would be despatched on 30th December. That was the final date. Their team was already there at the site and they
had to do 72-hour mechanical test. So there had been initial delays, which they have not been able to catch up, but they
would catch up with that so that there was no further delay.
9.4       Thereafter, the Convenor observed that their progress was not up to the mark. The Committee was trying to do
three things (1) if the company was not a fit venture, it should be wound up; (2) if it otherwise was good for profit the
Committee would recommend it for help; (3) if it was good then the Committee would assist in amalgamation, mergers
etc. The Committee did not want other companies to suffer. Inefficiency of one should not reflect on the other.
9.5       The representative of Bharat Petroleum informed that with BYNL 18 orders for Rs. 170 crores were currently in
execution. They did help them financially. Till current date the progress was in order.
9.6       Representative of Hindustan Petroleum informed that they had been helping BYNL in general. Time delay was
an issue. In their Bombay refinery they placed an order on BHPV for a 50 tonne boiler. However, it was not delivering
what was it supposed to do and even after commissioning BHPV was rectifying that.
9.7       Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas, informed that the problem arose because there was lack of coordination
between their ministry and BYNL companies. Now this would be sorted out in the monthly meeting of the two
secretaries. He further informed that the problems of finance, delays and Liquidated Damages will be brought before the
independent bodies of the Board which would be consisted of independent and non-official directors. The independent
bodies would look at it with an open mind and come out with a recommendation. It was hoped that something would
come out of that exercise.
9.8       The Convenor enquired as to whether a One Time Settlement could be had to help the BYNL companies.
Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas, informed that it was possible for the Government to write off its dues. It was not
possible for the Government to wave dues of a corporation. The objective was that BYNL should continue to get orders.
The second is that they should continue to do well and they should not face difficulty in executing work because of lack
of finances. They were already getting the orders. In case there were any difficulties because of the lack of finances,
when both secretaries meet in the monthly meetings, they would have a discussion and see that there were no difficulties
in executing the orders. Thirdly, the Liquidating Damages question should be seen by an independent director. If this
mechanism was allowed to work for a year, it was hoped that the objective of BYNL would be achieved and time gap
reduced. When Convenor enquired whether they could do something about waiving off LDs upto March 2001,
Secretary, Petroleum and Natural Gas, informed that they had taken up matter to the Boards but the Boards had not
agreed to waive the Liquidated Damages. Although ONGC had argued the case in a fair manner but since ONGC had

107th Report of Committee on Industry

suffered losses so they could not compound their losses by waiving the penalty on an organisation that had caused the
loss.
9.9       The Convenor observed that in the interest of the industry and country, both the secretaries should spend a lot of
time to resolve the issue. He opined that as a One Time Settlement, substantial amount of LDs should be waived upto
March 31, 2001 taking a cue from Government decision that have been done in the case of UTI and IDBI. The
Committee's decision was to be taken to Board and they may be conveyed the concern of the Committee in this matter.
The Convenor strongly felt that in case the Committee's recommendation was accepted by the Boards, the Committee
would not call meetings time and again to review the issue and everything would be left to the Secretaries of Heavy
Industry and Petroleum & Natural Gas.
CHAPTER–III
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10.       The Committee noted that both the Secretaries of Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and
Petroleum and Natural Gas would have monthly meetings to sort out the problems of finance and delays and Liquidated
Damages would be brought before the independent bodies of the Boards (consisting of independent and non-official
Directors) and those independent bodies would look at it with an open mind. The Committee also observed during the
course of the meetings with various PSUs that delays were sometimes due to involvement of various parties like the
projects of Gandhar where ONGC, Engineering Project India Ltd., Bharat Pumps and Compressors Ltd. and holding
company BYNL had to sort out the problem arising due to supply and testing of compressors. Delays also occurred due
to change in specifications. The Committee also noted that sometimes delays occurred due to labour problem
particularly in the State of Bihar and insurgency problems in Assam. Delays also took place due to delay in importing
engines from abroad due to difficulty in opening Letter of Credit by the supplier company. The Committee feels the Oil
Boards should go into all these aspects and consider the cases where delays on part of the supplier did not contribute to
additional delay before imposing LDs. The Committee recommends that both the Secretaries should look into the details
in their monthly meetings keeping in view the feelings of the Committee. The Committee also recommends that a
quarterly report may be submitted to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry about the
finance, delays and LDs.
11.       The Committee noted during the deliberation that delay in fabrication, supply and commissioning of equipments
contributed to the overall delay in timely completion of the projects. The Committee observes that now delays should be
avoided at all costs. The Committee recommends that a mechanism should be found out by the Department of Heavy
Industry to monitor the work chart of the supplier company and corrective measure should be taken in case delay
occurred at the incipient stage before the delay has any damaging effect on the ongoing project.
12.       Keeping in view the overall industrial scenario, the Committee supports the viewpoint of DHI made by them at
its meeting held on 13th August, 2002 on capacity building in the country itself as the country is opening up and it
would have a different kind of import regime. Companies would be coming to Petroleum sector and construction sector,
and therefore, user sector and capital goods sector should help each other in building a certain capacity to reap benefit of
the new situation.
13.       The Committee strongly feels that in the national interest, a One Time Settlement should be worked out and
substantial amount of LDs may be waived upto 31 March, 2001 to improve the ways and means of Indian companies
taking a cue from the Government decision that has been taken in the case of UTI and IDBI. The Committee strongly
recommends that its concern may be conveyed to the Oil Boards and they may be impressed upon to have a
sympathetic look at the matter. The Committee further observes that in case problems relating to LDs upto 31st
March, 2001 are settled amicably, the Committee would not dilate the matter further and leave it to the
Secretaries of both the Ministries.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Departme nt-related Parliamentary Standing  Committee on Industry, having been
authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundre d-eighth Report on the Acti on Taken by the Government 
on the recommendations contained in the 91st Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry on Coir Board---A Performance Review pertaining to Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries. 
2.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered  and adopted the Draft report
at its meeting held on the 17th December, 2002. 
3.      The 91st Report of the Department-related Parl iamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to the 
Hon'ble Chairman Rajya Sabha on 20th August, 2002 and to Rajya Sabha on 11th December, 2002 and laid on the
Table of Lok Sabha on 11th December, 2002.
 
REPORT 
        The One Hundred-eighth Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
