          The Committee recommends that unless State Governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for
industries, integration and harmonization of villages with industrial development cannot be achieved. Active
participation of State Governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial Policy announced in 1991, to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small, tiny and village
industries.                                                                                                 (Para 21.3)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that Comptroller and Auditor General should be advised to devise some
system so that the payments due to SSI are automatically paid within a specified time.       (Para 22.4)
          The Committee is of the opinion that the timely payment to SSIs could be ensured by issuing an appropriate
circular of the Ministry of Finance for the Ministries/Departments at least of the Central Government. The Central
Government should also impress upon the State Governments to take similar measures to expedite payments to
SSIs.                       (Para 22.5)
          The Committee reiterates its recommendation that stringent action should be taken against the erring large
companies which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time. Necessary amendment for taking punitive action
may also be contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.                                                                      (Para 22.6)
          The Committee reiterates its recommendation, made in its 75th Report, that in order to protect small scale sector
from multinational companies and others, a certain per cent of items, say 33% should be purchased from SSI sector by
Central and State Government Departments/Agencies specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been
withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL list. The policy of purchase preference system as followed
by USA Government for protection of indigenous industries may be emulated. Necessary action in this regard should be
initiated by the Ministry of SSI immediately.                                                                                                             (Para
24.2)
          A mention has been made about the Partnership Act in the Union Budget 2003-04 and the Ministry of SSI is
addressing the matter. The Committee desires that the legislation should be enacted without much delay.                        
                  (Para 25.2)
          From the oral evidence rendered before the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry by
various SSI Associations, it appears that the impact of the above activities have not been as it should have been. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that activities like seminars/workshops should be intensified to bring adequate
awareness among the SSI entrepreneurs.                                                                                          (Para 26.5)
          The Committee recommends that the Comprehensive law should be enacted. It should be an encompassing one
and should enable the SSI Sector to come out of the clutches of inspector raj. The Committee is of the opinion that
inspector raj has persisted despite attempt at the higher level to change it and time has come to enact suitable legislative
action to bring the inspector raj to an end.                                                                                                    (Para 27.3)
            In view of the replies received from the Ministry, the Committee hopes that the problems could be sorted out
with the Uttar Pradesh Financial Corporation as informed by the Ministry of
SSI.                                                                                                                             (Para 28.2)

also stressed that the percentage of equity participation should be increased from 24% to 49% as recommended in S.B.
Gupta Committee Report.

mentioned about the new Securities Act which has granted huge powers to the bank managers who have become
indifferent to the plight of small scale industrialist. He also opined that interest rate should be lowered and there should

recovery tribunal. He also stated that incentives in the form of marketing development assistance should be increased to
remove the problems of the exporters.

`Sickness in SSI Sector in the city of Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh' which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 11th December, 2002.
 
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorised as follows :-
 
(i)
                  Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government :- Paras 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 1.10 and 1.11 (Chapter - I)
 
(ii)        Recommendations/Observations, which   the Committee does not desire to pursue in  view  of  the Government's replies :- Paras 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7  (Chapter-II).

3.15, 3.16, 3.17 and 3.18 (Chapter-III).
 
(v)
               Recommendations/Observations of the Committee have been placed separately. (Chapter-IV).
 
3.         The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has accepted its recommendations as mentioned in Chapter - I of the Report.

CHAPTER – I
 
LABOUR REFORMS IN SSI SECTOR
 
Recommendation
 
1.1       The Associations brought it to the notice of the Committee that the Union Finance Minister had assured that units employing less than one thousand persons would not be brought under the ambit of labour laws, but in
reality, when these units are required to resize their manpower, they are not able to do it as the employees go in for arbitration where dates of hearing are fixed six months after filing the application.  When labour is given
some rights, they start misbehaving with the management.  Management of SSI units spend a lot of time in solving the problems posed by the labourers.  In Kanpur 90 per cent of SSI units have become sick due to leadership
of labour.  There is no power in the hands of the management to discipline the labour.
 
Wherever the statutory dues were paid in the industry, sickness started to surface and whenever workers were made permanent, they stopped doing work and started misbehaviour with the management.  Labour
reforms should, therefore, be done in a way so that the constraints coming in the way of running units could be removed.  Hire and Fire system may be one of the options  which can be considered by the Government. 
(Para  2.3)
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Amendment proposals in the Industrial Disputes Act,1947 are under consideration of the Government as informed by Ministry of Labour which deals with the issue.
 
 
PROVISIION FOR TESTING FACILITY
 
1.2            Recommendation
 
There is no provision for a testing facility in Kanpur for the paint industry. Consequently, they have to go to Kolkata for getting their products tested. To an enquiry the Association informed that IIT and CIGS do not
have any provision for testing facilities for SSI units. These institutions cater to the needs of the defence sector only. Even if SSI sector get any tests done at these institutions, the test results are not accepted by other
organizations like Railways, etc. The Associations, therefore, requested for providing a testing facility for the paint industry.
(Para  2.5)
 
Action taken by the Government

            The Regional Testing Centre (NR), New Delhi is having complete testing facilities for testing paints, enamels, dry distemper, varnish, solvents, thinners, pigments and extenders as per relevant Indian Standards. This
Centre provides services to all small scale industrial units located in the northern region of the country, which include the State of UP. Small scale industrial units located in Kanpur can avail the testing facilities for getting
their products tested at RTC, New Delhi. It is further stated that concessional testing charges are levied for test samples received from registered small scale industrial units. The laboratories of Regional Testing Centre(NR),
New Delhi are having  recognition from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), New Delhi and accreditation with the NABL, Department of Science & Technology, Govt. of India, New Delhi.  SISI, Kanpur has been advised
to disseminate the information on test facilities available at the Centre regarding paints, varnishes, etc. and motivate the SSI units to take advantage of these testing facilities.
 
BANKING OMBUDSMAN SCHEME
 
1.3            Recommendation
 
Even if an industry falls sick, it does not mean that it will not survive.  If the proper aid is given to the industry at the initial stage of sickness, it can survive.  The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has given a guideline for
assessing the sickness of SSI but it is on paper only.  The banks and Financial Institutions (FIs) are not adhering to it.  It should be mandatory for the banks/ Financial Institutions to adhere to the RBI guidelines regarding
assessment of sickness of industries.  There should be an ombudsman with whom complaints against banks/ Financial Institutions can be registered.
Para  2.12
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The detailed guidelines have been issued by RBI to all scheduled commercial banks for implementation, wherein banks have been advised to take a sympathetic attitude and strive for rehabilitation in respect of viable
SSI units, particularly wherever the sickness is on account of circumstances beyond the control of entrepreneurs.  The guidelines also provide for a mechanism for early detection of sickness in SSI units and the package for
rehabilitation of such units for implementation by the financing banks.
 
The RBI has advised the banks to implement the guidelines fully and to submit a report to their Boards on the progress made in assisting the SSI units under the new guidelines.
 
            The Banking Ombudsman Scheme exits which covers aspects relating to non-observance of RBI directives on interest rates, delays in sanction, disbursement or non-observance of prescribed time schedule for
disposal of loan applications, etc. The RBI has given directives that banks should comply with the Banking Ombudsman Scheme.
 
 
TELECOM NETWORK
 
1.4            Recommendation
 
Poor telecom network in semi-urban areas sometimes prove to be a hindrance for SSI units.  A little communication gap between the supplier and the client due to absence of proper telecommunication system may
result in business loss.
Para  2.14
 
Action taken by the Government
 
With infrastructure growth in the communications sector, telecom services, Internet services, etc. have expanded vastly reaching even to semi-urban and rural areas.  The telecommunication system has improved
considerably and SSI entrepreneurs should not find any major difficulties in accessing the services.
 
MINIMUM WAGES
 
1.5            Recommendation
 
Industrial unrest and wages are inter-linked.  If the industry is using skilled labour, it cannot be engaged on minimum wages.  Wages are determined by demand and supply.  Skilled workers will go to an industry
where  they get higher wages.  If the industry sticks to the stipulated minimum wages, it will give rise to industrial unrest, which will hamper working of the industry.  Government should make a fresh survey to define
minimum wages.
Para  2.16
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Ministry of Labour has informed that the Minimum Wages Act,1948 provides for fixation, revision and enforcement of minimum wages of the workers engaged in the scheduled employments both in the Central and
State sphere mostly in the unorganized sector. The Act safeguards the interests of these workers, as they are susceptible to exploitation due to illiteracy and lack of bargaining power. The Act binds the employers to pay the
minimum wages fixed under the Act. The minimum wages are fixed and revised separately for highly skilled, skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers. The rates of wages of the workers are fixed at higher level with the
rise in merits of the skills.
 
PURCHASE PREFERENCE POLICY FOR SSI
 
1.6            Recommendation
 
Government institutions are not giving priority to SSIs in the matter of purchase of various items, Government bodies are purchasing items from outside the state although the same items are available in the state at
competitive rates.
 
Action taken by the Government

WORKSHOP IN KANPUR
 
1.7            Recommendation
 
The Committee desired that the Ministry should reach the grass-root level and for this purpose, it should hold regular orientation courses, seminar, workshop etc. in Kanpur.  The Committee hopes that this kind of
action would enable the SSIs to reap benefit of the schemes formulated for them by the Government of India.
Para  4.1
 
Action taken by the Government
 
SISI, Kanpur has been organizing Skill Development Programmes, Industrial motivational campaigns, Entrepreneurship Development Programmes, Management Development Programmes, Vendor Development
Prgrammes, Buyer Seller Meets, etc. on a regular basis at Kanpur. Besides, Awareness Programmes/ Workshops, Training Programme on Packaging for Exports/ISO 9000, Sensitization Programme on WTO, etc. are also
organized. These programmes are organized in collaboration with the concerned Central/ State Departments and information on the various schemes being implemented for the promotion and development of SSIs is
provided for the benefit of SSI entrepreneurs/participants.
 
 
MONITORING OF CREDIT FLOW TO SSIT SECTOR
 
1.8            Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that there was some mismatch between the RBI figures and the associations contention about the non-availability of credit.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries should strictly monitor the credit flow to SSIs so that the true picture in this regard emerges.
Para  4.2
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            The Reserve Banks of India (RBI) regulates the scheduled commercial banks and is therefore, is the only authentic source of information on credit flow to the SSI sector from the commercial banks.  The data on
advances to the sector by the various banks is compiled and monitored at the RBI level. 
 
            In order to have a constant and focused vigil on flow of credit to SSI and address the problems faced by the sector in securing adequate credit, etc. the RBI has constituted the Standing Advisory Committee to review
flow of Institutional Credit to SSI sector under the Chairmanship of the Deputy Governor, RBI.  The representatives of SSI Associations are also members in this Committee. The Committee inter-alia reviews the flow of
credit to the SSI sector and problems faced by the sector in securing an adequate flow of credit. Therefore, it may be seen that there is a transparency in the mechanism of monitoring of credit flow to the SSI sector wherein
the SSI Associations are given the opportunity to give their views or suggestions.    
 
DISPOSAL OF LOAN APPLICATIONS IN BANKS
 
1.9            Recommendation
 
The Committee recommends that the banks should give receipt to the applicant  after taking the application and inform the applicant within two months the reasons for rejecting the application.  Banks should be
persuaded to be SSI friendly.  As regards non-supply of required financial data by the applicants, the banks should give the applicant proper counselling at the initial stage of the scrutiny of the application.
Para  4.3
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The RBI has advised the banks that a clear cut monitoring system may be laid down which captured the process of sanctioning loan from the receipt of application to sanction or rejection and the reasons for rejection.
The banks  have also been advised to prepare the necessary ‘Check List’ and circulate it among the controlling offices and branches to make available the same to the potential borrower while giving the loan application
forms.
Further, the RBI has recently instructed the banks to dispose off loans up to Rs.25,000 within 2 weeks and in other cases for loans up to Rs. 5 lakhs within a period of 4 weeks on receipt of loan applications complete
in all respects and duly accompanied by a check list. All such loan applications which are complete in all respects and accompanied by a check list should also be acknowledged by the bank branches on the same day i.e. on
the day the application is received by the branch.
 
ROLE OF LEAD BANKS
 
1.10            Recommendation
 
The Committee further recommends that all the lead banks should have interaction with the State Industries’ Association on regular basis regarding credit and its recovery etc.  and the decisions taken in the meeting
may be conveyed to the Ministry of SSI and RBI for further necessary action.
Para  4.4

IMPROVING CD RATIO OF UTTAR PRADESH
 
1.11            Recommendation
 
As regards the CD ratio of Uttar Pradesh, the Committee observes that the ratio is much below the desired level.  The Committee desires that Ministry of SSI and RBI should impress upon the State Government to
find ways and means for increasing the level of CD ratio in the State.
Para  4.8
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            The RBI has informed that the State Government has been impressed upon to initiate measures for improving CD ratio by critically reviewing in different fora such as SLBC/ DCC/DLRC.             Bank of Baroda has
informed that being Convenor of SLBC in State of U.P., the Bank has taken the initiative and discussed the issue in various SLBC meetings and formed a core group of SLBC for C.D. Ratio in January,2002. Core group of

CHAPTER – II
 
RECOVERY OF LOAN
 
2.1            Recommendation
 
Banks have no mechanism to recover loans.  State Finance Corporations have the right under the Provision of Arrears of Land Revenue to sell the closed unit to another unit to recover the amount of loan.  In case of
banks, the matter goes to the Debt Recovery Tribunal and the condition of machines purchased by the sick units becomes worse due to non-use.  To obviate the situation, the banks should be given the right to sell the
defaulter unit.  This would encourage the banks to give loans, as there would be a way to recover the loan.
Para  2.11
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            In case of conduct of SSI accounts becoming unsatisfactory and the borrowers failing to regularize the position despite notices from the bank, the loan can be called up and recovery suit can be filed against the
borrower to recover the loans.
 
            “The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Ordinance, 2002 repromulgated on 21.8.2002 provides that in case of default in repayment of secured debt by
borrower and the account in respect of such debt being classified as non-performing asset, the secured creditor may require the borrower through notice to discharge full liabilities within 60 days and in the event of borrower
failing to discharge the liabilities, the secured creditor may take over possession of secured assets (including the right to transfer, assignment or sale) for realizing the secured asset and / or  take over the management  of
secured assets and realize the secured assets,  appoint a manager to manage the secured assets, require any person who acquired the secured assets from the borrower from whom money is due to pay to the secured creditor
money sufficient to pay the secured debt. (The Ordinance has since been passed by both the Houses of the Parliament in Winter Session 2002).
 
Where dues of the secured creditor are not fully satisfied with the sale proceeds of secured assets, the secured creditor may file an application  to the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) or a competent Court for recovery
of the balance amount from the borrower.  
 
EPF & ESI SCHEMES
 
2.2            Recommendation
 
Some deductions are made from the salaries of the labourers on account of Provident Fund.  But when the labourers change one unit after another, in most cases they do not get their dues due to non-availability of
records.  It is, therefore, suggested that the employees may be issued passbooks and entries relating to amount deducted from their salaries may be entered in them.  They would be able to receive their dues from the units
from which they retire on this factual basis.
In the case of ESIC, the benefits go to the owner or director of the unit and not to workers.  A policy should be evolved so that workers get their benefit and owners pay the premium for the same.
Para  2.18
 
Action taken by the Government

The Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme,1952 provides for issue of passbooks to employers to suit the requirements of their employees. Further, Account Slips are issued every year to members showing opening
balance, contribution received during the year and interest earned on such contribution. Also, to resolve the problem reported, Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) has already initiated the process for issue of
Social Security Number (SSN).  On allotment of the unique SSN, this problem may be solved since each worker will have only one unique number irrespective of the establishment(s) in which the member may be working.
 
The ESI Scheme under the ESI Act,1948 is a Contributory Scheme. It is mainly financed from Contribution by the Employees and Employers. The rate of contribution by employers is 4.75% of the wage wherein the
employee’s contribution is at the rate of 1.75% of the wage. The employees of factories/ establishments drawing wages not exceeding Rs. 6500/- P.M. are covered under the ESI Scheme. Workers who are covered under the
ESI Scheme are entitled to medical care and cash benefits in the contingency of sickness/maternity/ disablement and death due to employment, under the ESI Act. Contributions are payable by the Principal employers of
factory/establishments. However, he is authorized to recover from the wages and not otherwise provided that no such deduction are to be made from any wages other than those relating to the period in respect of which the
contribution is payable. The employer is not entitled to recover the employer’s share of contribution from the wage of the employees.
 
TAXATION ON HOSIERY INDUSTRY
 
2.3            Recommendation
 
Four per cent taxation has been imposed on hosiery industry. Due to this, it has become sick. The rate of taxation should be uniform throughout the country and, like other states, the taxation rate should be one per
cent on this industry.
Para  2.22
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            Imposition of 4% sales tax on the hosiery industry is as per the uniform floor rates list of sales tax which has been unanimously adopted by all the State Governments as per the decision taken in the Conference of
Chief Ministers of States/ UTs held on 16
th November, 1999.  Ministry of Finance has informed that since the uniform floor rates list has been adopted by all the States, the 4% rate of sales tax on hosiery industry is uniform
throughout the country.

2.7            Recommendation
 
As regards labour problems, the Committee desires that SSI management should evolve ways and means to motivate labour for maximum productivity.  The Committee feels if labour is taken into confidence and is
apprised of the situation, they will lend their helping hand to the management for the overall benefit of the SSI Sector.
Para  4.9
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The SISIs impart training to entrepreneurs /workers under various entrepreneurship development/ management development programmes and skill development programmes. In these training programmes, training is
imparted even on behavioural aspects based on techniques for maintaining cordial and harmonious relations between management and workers on the one hand and amongst co-workers on the other hand and the need for
developing a harmonious relationship is emphasized.  The onus for motivating the labour lies on the management style and policies of the entrepreneurs. 
 
ANTI-SOCIAL ELEMENTS IN INDUSTRIAL AREAS
 
2.8            Recommendation
 
Due to power cut, anti-social elements are thriving in industrial areas. State police authority expresses their helplessness,as they do not have enough force to tackle the law and order situation there. The SSI branches
of banks are located outside the urban area of Kanpur. It is quite difficult to go to the SSI branch to deposit or collect money. Banks should be located in safe areas.
Para  2.21
 
Action taken by the Government
 
Maintenance of law and order primarily comes under the purview of the State Governments. After the nationalization of Banks, it was one of the basic objectives to expand the network of branches all over the country
and take banking to the remotest corner so that access to credit facilities becomes easier for various categories of borrowers including SSI borrowers.  Banks have been advised by the RBI to make concerted efforts to
operationalise at least one specialized SSI branch in every district and centres having clusters of SSI unit. As at the end of March, 2002, 395 specialised SSI branches of the public sector banks are functioning.  Further, banks
have been permitted to categorise their general banking branches having 60% or more of their advances to SSI sector as specialized SSI branches in order to encourage them to open more specialized SSI branches for
providing better service to this sector as a whole. 
 
COMMON EFFLUENT TREATMENT PLANT
 
2.9            Recommendation
 
Pollution control for the industries is necessary, but generally, problems keep on cropping up due to various reasons. Therefore, in industrial areas where SSIs are situated as a cluster, facilities should be provided by
the administration for setting up of a common effluent treatment plant.
Para  2.23

            To ensure prompt payment by large industries to small scale industrial units, the Government has enacted Interest on Delayed Payments to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act in 1993. The Act as

Recommendation
 
With the arrival of MNCs and concession given to Khadi industries, sickness in the soap industry commenced. The methodology and size of manpower required for hand made soap industry is the same in both the

SISI Kanpur will be organizing a Vendor Development Programme-cum-Exhibition with association of Railways in February, 2003. Railways will be requested to participate in the Programme and exhibit their spare
parts for the benefits of engineering industries.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee desires to know whether the said exhibition was actually held in February, 2003 and  if so,  whether any impact of the event has been assessed.
 
ACCEPTANCE OF PAYMENT IN SMALLER DENOMINATION BY BANKS
 
3.16            Recommendation
 
SSIs receive their payments in smaller denomination notes (like one, two or five) and coins. The banks do not accept these currencies. SSIs have to suffer the loss of approximately five per cent (brokerage) in
payment on the coins. RBI should give clear guidelines to banks to accept all types of currencies.
Para  2.27
 
Action taken by the Government
 
            RBI has advised that all commercial banks are instructed to accept and exchange notes in all denomination including smaller denomination. If any SSI unit faces problem in this regard, a specific complaint could be
made to RBI’s Kanpur Regional Office or directly to the Central Office.
 
            Bank of Baroda, Convenor of SLBC in State of U.P. has advised the Regions and branches under their control to adhere to the guidelines issued by the RBI with regard to acceptance of currency. The bank has also
informed that they have not received any complaint of such nature by their clients so far.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
The Committee is happy to note that RBI  has issued a guideline in the matter. The Committee desires that SSI associations may be informed of the RBI instructions given to the banks.
 
CHARGING OF INTEREST BY BANKS
           
3.17            Recommendation
 
The Committee has been informed that as per RBI’s recent instructions, NPAs are affected within three months of sanction of loan.  In addition, interest is charged every month, which in turn affects the credit
availability.  The Ministry of SSI has taken up the matter with the RBI.  The Committee recommends that government should look into the matter and come out with a suitable solution keeping in view the overall interest of
SSIs.
Para  4.7
 
Action taken by the Government
 
The RBI advised the banks to adopt 90 days’ norm for recognition of loan impairment from the year ending March 31,2004 and that they should move over to charging of interest on advances at monthly rests with
effect from April 1,2002. Ministry of SSI had taken up with the RBI the issues that 90 days’ over due norm for identification of NPAs would be disadvantageous for the SSIs and charging interest on monthly rests would
make credit costlier. The RBI has clarified that the above norm for recognition of loan impairment and the consequent charging of interest at monthly rests has been introduced after due consideration and in keeping with
international best practices. Since our financial system is also under scrutiny from various international agencies, it is not feasible to depart from these norms without affecting the confidence of the international and financial
capital markets. Besides, 90 days’ norm will come into effect only after a considerable lapse of time viz., March 31,2004 and hence both banks and the industry will have sufficient time to adjust to the new requirement.   
 
            The RBI has subsequently advised the banks in May,2002 that they should ensure that the effective rate does not go up merely on account of switchover to the system of charging of interest on monthly rests. The
banks have been advised not to compound interest at monthly rests till March31,2003.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION

REPORT
 
        The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel
management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of
PSEs. In fulfilling its roles, it associated itself with other Ministries and Organizations.
1.1   The important role and tasks of the Department of Public Enterprises are :
          (i)    General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (ii)   Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (iii)  Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage
settlement, training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
          (iv)  Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central PSEs under VRS;
          (v)   Matters relating to reservation of posts in PSEs to certain classes of citizens;
          (vi)  All matters relating to Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Public Sector Enterprises and the
Administrative Ministries/Departments;
          (vii)Matters relating to the delegation of powers to the Board of Directors;
          (viii)To undertake in-depth studies in respect of significant areas of functioning of Central PSEs;
          (ix)  Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE);
          (x)   Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE);
          (xi)  To monitor and evaluate the performance of PSEs and to act as a repository of data and to bring out an
Annual Survey for the Parliament;
          (xii)Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators for settlement of disputes among Public Sector Enterprises and
Government Departments except disputes relating to tax matters;

COUNSELLING RETRAINING AND REDPLOYMENT SCHEME
3.     The Scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment was introduced by Department of Public Enterprises
from the year 2001-02, and has been carried out continuously for the year 2002-03. The Scheme inter alia aims at
providing an opportunity of short duration orientation programme to the rationalised employees of Central PSEs. As per
the recent trends, on an average around 45,000 employees are being released under VRS/VSS every year. Further the
nodal training agencies selected for carrying out the CRR programme have also projected higher targets for the
coverage. However, considering the availability of the fund and in order to maximize the utilization of the resources,
targets are distributed among the agencies considering their capacity, potential to train and support the redeployment
drive. For carrying out the CRR programme, 17 nodal agencies were selected out of which 16 agencies were functional
during 2001-02. The number of nodal agencies have been increased from 17 to 25 during 2002-03. During 2001-02
selected nodal agencies were allowed to operate through 40 Employee Assistance Centres (EACs). The number of
EACs has increased to 80 during 2002-03.
3.1   The Department of Public Enterprises has apprised that considering the need to have flexibility and also economy
of the scale, the training has been distributed in 20 days/30 days/40 days module depending upon trade/skill being opted
by the rationalized employees. The projection under the CRR programme is made on year-to-year basis. For the year
2001-02, against a projection of 8000 employees to be trained, 8423 persons were trained. For the year 2002-03, there is
a projection to train 10,000 persons and it is likely to meet the target as per available trends being received from the
agencies. For the year 2003-04, it is projected to meet a target of Rs. 11,000 person. The Expenditure Norms per person
are separate for 20 days/30 days/40 days modules of training. Similarly, a separate element of sensitization programme
for providing 3 days counselling camp in the vicinity of the PSU has been made available under the CRR programme so
as to provide the basic inputs, counsel the employees prior to their release from the organizations and to assess the
training needs so as to enable  them to rejoin the productive process once they part with the CPSU.
3.2   With regard to monitoring mechanism, agencies have been asked to submit the batchwise information for the
training undertaken, the progress on redeployment of the persons so trained etc. Besides, the officials of CRR Cell, DPE
also inspects the site of the training, inter-act with the participants. In order to support the mechanism, endeavour has
also been made to set up the Coordination Committees consisting of Members of Central PSEs in the vicinity, lead bank
managers and the nodal agencies carrying out the programme so that some of the basic issues could be discussed locally
and the CRR programme could be monitored at the local level by the said Committee.
3.3   Out of the total plan allocation of Rs. 10.00 crores in BE 2003-04, the major part of it i.e. 9.00 crores is for
Retraining and Redeployment of rationalized workers of CPUs. The Ministry has apprised that the Plan allocation of Rs.
8.50 crore was made in 2002-03 (RE) and in B.E. 2003-04, Rs. 9 crores has been allocated for the implementation of the
Scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment of rationalised employees of CPSUs.
3.4   The Committee finds that there has been constant increase in the plan allocation of CRR Scheme over the
earlier years. As against Rs. 6.75 crores allocated in RE 2001-02, an allocation of Rs. 8.50 crores was made in BE
2002-03 for CRR which was taken up by DPE since 1st April, 2001. Earlier it was dealt by the Department of
Industrial Policy and Promotion. In BE 2003-04, the amount has been increased to Rs. 9.00 crores. This is the
third year since the scheme commenced. The Committee recommends that in view of the increasing trends in the
plan allocation for CRR scheme and time factor, a suitable mechanism for appraisal of the scheme should be
evolved by DPE so as to evaluate the results in this regard and assess the desired impact of the scheme.
3.5   During the year 2003-04, the Plan allocation is of Rs. 10 crore of which 10% has been earmarked for North East
(NE) Region and the balance i.e. Rs. 9 crore is for the CRR programme for other regions inclusive of project monitoring
element. The allocations for the year 2001-02 was Rs. 8 crore. Of this, 10% i.e. Rs. 0.80 crore was earmarked for NE
Region and the balance of Rs. 7.20 crore for CRR programme for other regions including project monitoring. For

of VRS and who are willing and eligible being within 58 years of age are selected by the Nodal Agencies after a
thorough counselling and within the target set for these agencies based on the availability of the fund. The trainees
themselves decide the area of training. Nodal agencies help them in identifying the areas having potential to set up new
ventures. The ex-employees of those PSEs, which are located in and around the location of the training centres, are
invited for the programme. Department of Public Enterprises is in the process of preparation of the list of the trainees,
PSE-wise.
3.8   The Committee in its 73rd report on Demands for Grants (2002-03) also dealt with the CRR scheme and observed
as under :
        "The Committee, however, observes that there may be cases where V.R.S. optees are in the age group of 50-57 and
by human nature they stop learning any new trade and imparting training to them would only result in waste of
time and Government money. The Committee, therefore, recommends that provision may be made for giving
training to the sons/daughters of such persons and that too before they are retired."
        The Ministry in their action taken note stated as under :
        "The recommendations of the Committee in regard to providing the facilities under the CRR programme to the
sons/daughters of the VRS optees who are in the age group of 50-57 have been noted. Considering the human
angle, as recommended by the Hon'ble Members, the matter would be taken up for consideration appropriately."
        The issue was again raised by the Chairman in the course of deliberation with the Secretary, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. The Secretary stated the following :
        "As far as wards part is concerned, we have this suggestion with us. It is under examination. We will certainly
come back to you sooner than later whether we can include the wards in the training part, where the separated
employee is not able to undertake the training. This is under active consideration of the Ministry."
3.9   The Committee observes that the issue has been under consideration of the Ministry for the last one year
and a decision is yet to be taken. By that time, about 20,000 employees would have completed training. This
lukewarm approach needs to be put into the right perspective. The Committee, therefore, recommends that an
early decision may be expedited in the matter for the benefit of VRS optees.
3.10The counselling and training programmes is planned in order to equip VRS optees with skills and orientation to
engage themselves in self-employment activities and rejoin the productive process even after their separation from the
CPSUs. The aim is to provide alternative employment opportunities to the VRS/VSS opted employees of the PSEs.
However, the skill they possess is of the different nature i.e. they have the experience of working under the PSU of a
Heavy Industry where the employment opportunity has ceased to exist. However, on retirement they would need the
skill of different name for setting up their own venture a small scale business. In order to overcome this gap, DPE
should co-ordinate with the Ministry of SSI to offer them training. The Committee also feels the need of adequate funds
for such employees to start there own vocation. Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises in course
of his deliberation before the Committee on 20th March, 2003 stated that under this scheme, which started last year, an
allocation of Rs. 8.5 crores was made. This year an allocation of Rs. 10 crores has been made. This allocation falls short
of the demand as far as this scheme is concerned. One of the problems faced by the workers who have been separated is

3.11The Committee, therefore, recommends that training for VRS optee employees should be organized in such a
way that they can create self-employment in the small scale sector and avail the benefit of the schemes like
PMRY, REGP etc. in the small and tiny sector. Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) scheme has
now taken roots. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to increase its spread to cover at least 40,000
workers per annum in addition to covering a backlog of about 1 lakh workers. In this context, the Committee
recommends that steps are urgently required for allocation of funds for the scheme which needs to be at least
doubled. Ministry of Heavy Industries should also ensure that PSEs shall clear all their dues before relieving
them from the organization so that they can plan their future course of action in earning livelihood in the new
environment. Ministry of Finance should issue direction that banks honour their financial requirements in the
aftermath of VRS/VSS to avail of the small sector employment schemes. The workers separated on VRS should
be entitled to borrowing from commercial banks under the priority sector lending dispensation.
3.12The Committee came to know that currently workers separated on VRS instantly loses the medical cover granted to
him under ESI Scheme. In case of natural superannuation, however, workers get an opportunity to continue the medical
benefits at their option and on requisite payment. The Committee strongly recommends that medical cover should
be granted to the workers being separated on VRS/VSS at least for a period of five years or till the date of
natural superannuation whichever is earlier. Ministry of Heavy Industries should devise a scheme in this regard
in consultation with all stakeholders.

MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
7.     MoU is a freely negotiated agreement between the public enterprise and the administrative ministry. Under the
agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the year. The MoU
covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system performance of the
Company is categorized into five categories namely : excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
7.1   All PSEs that have not been referred to the BIFR and are not insignificant in size are expected to sign an MoU. The
objectives of the MoU system are to :
        l   Improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management.
        l   Remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives the enterprise is to pursue through clearly laid down
performance targets at the beginning of the year in an MoU entered into between Chief Executive and
Secretary of the Administrative Ministry.
7.2   The MoU system has grown at a steady rate and from 4 MoUs signed in the year 1987-88, 107 MoUs were signed
for the year 2000-2001. In fact many of these 107 PSEs are the holding Companies and if their subsidiaries are also
included then the total No. of PSEs covered under MoU system works out to be as 163. The number of MoUs
signed/finalised since the inception of the MoU system are as follows :

7.6   The Committee recommends that DPE should reorient and reorganize its activities as far as signing of MoU

the MoU parameters while grading their performance and suggests to the Administrative Ministries in

which has nothing to offer for improvement of PSEs.

7.9   All the MoU signing PSEs are eligible to exercise certain financial and administrative autonomy so that they are
able to carry out their day to day operations more efficiently. At present there is no proposal under consideration to
grant full functional autonomy to the Boards of the PSEs. The Department of Public Enterprises would continue to act
as nodal Department to coordinate general policy framework relating to public sector enterprises.
7.10The Task Force on MoU system which is a body of experts helps the Department of Public Enterprises in the
process of finalising the MoUs of different PSEs operating in different areas by way of providing technical
expertise/inputs. The Task Force consists of retired Secretaries to Government of India, retired Chief Executives,

Professionals, and Academicians. In order to meet the requirements of technical inputs the Task Force has been

7.11The following steps have been taken by Department of Public Enterprises to make the MoU system more effective.
        (i)  Instead of confining the scope of MoU system to the traditional approach of arriving at certain figures under the

productivity, customer satisfaction, HRD, quality improvement and R&D to be included as prominent
performance indicators.
        (ii)The parameter on project implementation with suitable weight is required to be included in the draft MoUs.

consultation with the Administrative Ministries.
        (iv)Efforts have been made to finalize all MoUs before the commencement of the next financial year, so that the

coherent strategies to achieve those targets.
        (v)  In order to make the MoU negotiation meetings more meaningful and effective, it is ensured that the
participation from the Administrative Ministries/Departments is at a senior (Additional/Joint Secretary)
level.
7.12Some of the measures of financial and operational autonomy delegated to Boards of MoU signing PSEs are as
follows :
        1.   Capital Expenditure : MoU signing PSEs having Gross Block of over Rs. 200 crores can incur expenditure of
Rs. 50 crores on additions, modifications and new investments and Rs. 100 crores on replacement, renewal
of assets without prior approval of the Government provided they meet certain conditions.
        2.   Wage Revision : MoU signing PSEs can finalize wage revisions within broad guidelines laid down by DPE.
        3.   Incentive Scheme : MoU signing PSEs can evolve incentive schemes within the broad guidelines laid down by
DPE subject to the condition that the total of bonus and incentive shall not exceed to the 35% of the wages.
        4.   Transfer of Functional Directors : MoU signing PSEs have powers to transfer functional directors from one
charge to another in consultation with the Secretary of the Administrative Ministry and with the prior
approval of the Minister.
7.13The Committee observes that the investment decisions to create public sector units were based on social cost
benefit analysis. Moreover most of the public sector enterprises were not expected to maximize profits. However,
the social cause no longer being a vogue, and market forces replacing the old economy with the ushering in of
liberalization, the performance of PSEs has to be evaluated on their economic performance. The Public Sector
Enterprises's performance, therefore, should be evaluated based on their financial profit.
7.14MoU should have relation to financial well being of a PSEs. Financial parameters are must to evaluate the
state of health of a PSE. However, the Committee observes that PSEs which are even under performing are
graded as good, very good or excellent depending upon the level of their achievements under the MoU target.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that financial performance of PSEs should be the main criteria for
rating their achievement.
7.15The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad hoc Task Force on the basis
of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the target by the predetermined
stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as 'excellent' and when the target is just met, the enterprise is ranked as 'very
good'. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either 'good' or 'fair' or 'poor'. Ranking
depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
7.16The Committee appreciates the efforts of DPE to make the MoU system more effective. Still much more has
to be done in this direction. It is more important that dynamic parameters like productivity, customer
satisfaction, HRD, quality improvement and R&D are taken into account. Department of Public Enterprises

NON-OFFICIAL DIRECTORS IN BOARDS OF PSEs
8.     Part-time non-official Directors are individuals of repute having experience in different fields. On their
appointment as Directors the Boards of these PSEs get the benefit of their guidance and advice in the management of
the Company. Their appointment has helped in introducing transparent and effective systems of internal monitoring
through Audit Committees. The performance of PSEs depends upon a number of other critical factors such as its
competitive strength, organisational structure, the changes in its business environment, etc. Thus, it would be very
difficult to correctly quantify the improvement in performance of PSEs due to the delegation of powers mentioned
above. But enhanced autonomy to the PSEs certainly helps the managements to take quick decisions which are very
essential to meet the challenges of business especially under the emerging competitive economic environment.
8.1   Instructions have been issued by the Department of Public Enterprises to induct non-official part-time Directors on
the Boards of PSEs. The non-official Directors are drawn from public men, technocrats, management experts and
consultants, and professional managers in industry and trade with high degree of proven ability. The number of such
Directors should be at one-third of the actual strength of the Board. In the cases of listed Companies headed by
Executive Chairman, the number of non-official (Independent) Directors should be half of the Board.
8.2   The Navratna and Miniratna PSEs can exercise the enhanced powers only after their Boards and professionalised
by inducting adequate number of non-official Directors. A Search Committee consisting of Chairman Public Enterprises
Selection Board (PSEB), Secretary (DPE), Secretary of the Administrative Ministry concerned and eminent persons
from outside has been set up for selection of non-official Directors for the Navratna and Miniratna PSEs. The Search
Committee has been meeting frequently to make selections of non-official Directors.
8.3   Enhanced operational and financial powers are delegated to Navratna PSEs and Miniratnas. The enhanced power
enables these PSEs to take decisions in investment and operational matters without having to seek the approval of the
Government apart from cutting down delay in decision making, the efficiency as well as accountability of the Boards of
Directors have increased due to delegations of these powers. The enhanced powers are not available to sick PSEs.
8.4   The Committee observes that non-official part-time directors are drawn from various segments of society
i.e. public men, technocrats, management experts etc. However, they discharge their duties for no monetary gain.
Committee has the apprehension that this may play down on their accountability to the Board of PSE of which
they are members. DPE should look into this aspect.
PURCHASE  PREFERENCE  POLICY
9.     The Purchase reference Policy has been extended upto 31.3.2004. The Committee had earlier recommended that
Department of Public Enterprises should apprise the Committee about non-implementation of the policy, if any, by any
PSE. But Department of Public Enterprises have not so far complied with the recommendation. The Committee
understands that certain PSEs are not adhering to the Policy. Violation of the Policy by PSEs makes mockery of the
Policy which have been notified with the cabinet approval.
9.1   The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should apprise the Committee about the
non-implementation of the Policy for the last one year.
VOLUNTARY  RETIREMENT  SCHEME
10.   In the present system, funds are allocated to the central PSEs at 17.5% rate of interest per annum in case of
working capital loans including funds for VRS and at 13.5% rate of interest for other loans. In the falling interest rate
regime, transfer of such high cost funds severely impacts the balance sheet position of each PSE precipitating financial
crises. The Committee feels such high rate of interest attached to VRS funds have an adverse effect on the balance sheet
of the companies and it should be corrected.
10.1The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should revert to the old system of permitting VRS funds
as grants. It would be a much needed relief as loss making and marginally profit making companies are in urgent
need of shedding their oversized manpower.

        The Committee observes that at present there are 240 Central Public Sector Enterprises. If the percentage figure of
MoU signed PSEs is taken, it is less than 50% now. Sick PSEs are debarred from signing MoU. The Committee would
have appreciated if DPE would provide necessary logistical support like technical assistance to sick PSEs to revive and
rejuvenate them.                                                       (Para 7.8)
        The Committee observes that the investment decisions to create public sector units were based on social cost
benefit analysis. Moreover most of the public sector enterprises were not expected to maximize profits. However, the
social cause no longer being a vogue, and market forces replacing the old economy with the ushering in of
liberalization, the performance of PSEs has to be evaluated on their economic performance. The Public Sector
Enterprises's performance, therefore, should be evaluated based on their financial
profit.                                                                                            (Para 7.13)
        MoU should have relation to financial well being of a PSEs. Financial parameters are must to evaluate the state of
health of a PSE. However, the Committee observes that PSEs which are even under performing are graded as good, very
good or excellent depending upon the level of their achievements under the MoU target the Committee, therefore,
recommends that financial performance of PSEs should be the main criteria for rating their
achievement.                                                                                                        (Para 7.14)
        The Committee appreciates the efforts of DPE to make the MoU system more effective. Still much more has to be
done in this direction. It is more important that dynamic parameters like productivity, customer satisfaction, HRD,
quality improvement and R&D are taken into account. Department of Public Enterprises should constantly endeavour to
make MoU system as an instrument of improvement.(Para 7.16)
        The Committee observes that non-official part-time directors are drawn from various segments of society i.e.
public men, technocrats, management experts etc. However, they discharge their duties for no monetary gain.
Committee has the apprehension that this may play down on their accountability to the Board of PSE of which they are
members. DPE should look into this aspect.                                                          (Para 8.4)
        The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should apprise the Committee about the non-
implementation of the Policy for the last one year.  (Para 9.1)
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should revert to the old system of permitting VRS funds as
grants. It would be a much needed relief as loss making and marginally profit making companies are in urgent need of
shedding their oversized manpower.(Para10.1)

1.         The Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises) is responsible for promoting
engineering industry in the country and development and growth of capital goods.  The industries covered by this Department
provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the
requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping,
paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of  wide range of intermediate engineering
products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes.  There are 49  Public  Sector Enterprises (PSEs)
under the administrative charge of the Department.
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of engineering/capital goods,
consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department
of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8234.00 crores till 31st March, 2002,  employing about 1.18  lakh persons.
1.2       The Department holds interactions with various Industry Associations and evolves plans for the growth of the industry.
The Department also assists industry through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and trade, technological
collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

B.E. 2003-04. An allocation of Rs.25.00 crores under non-plan budget has also been made in B.E. 2003-04 for the purpose.
3.1       The allocated funds are to be utilized for funding significant projects on automotive safety and emission testing, on
creating infrastructure and validating performance of the components and  vehicles in terms of global emission, safety, tolerance
norms being prescribed by Economic Commission for Europe etc. Introduction of higher safety and emission norms is not
possible in the country without commensurate testing facilities being available. It is in this context that this allocation becomes
really meaningful and important.
3.2       Following delicensing of automotive industry in 1993, this sector has made great advances and has opened up to FDI.
The investment  in the industry is Rs.50,000 crores up to the end of March, 2000. The research activities in the automotive
sector have also comparatively intensified. All auto companies are having their own R&D laboratories to meet their limited
requirements. The infrastructure at Automotive Research Association of India, Pune, (ARAI), has also been considerably
upgraded to meet common requirements of all auto manufacturers. However, the total expenditure by auto industry at present on
its R&D activities is paltry 0.2 per cent. Considering the quality of automobiles in India as compared with the automobiles
manufactured in advanced countries, this expenditure on R&D is rather meager and needs to be increased considerably so that
the automobiles manufactured in India are of the same standard and quality as in developed countries. The improved quality of
automobiles will not only benefit the domestic consumers but will also enable the industry to export in larger numbers and
compete effectively.
3.3       The Government also has to provide financial assistance in this sector. The Committee notes that R&D has not received
the same importance it deserves in so far as allocation of funds is concerned. Although, tax holiday has been extended to R&D
companies up to March 31, 2004, but this measure is perhaps not adequate. What is required is enhanced allocation of funds 
collected as the cess on auto vehicles in order to intensify testing and research activities in the auto sector. The allocation to the
Ministry for R&D falls short of the projected demand i.e. Rs.1500 crores in the coming five to seven years. The Ministry was
allocated Rs.70 crores only during 2002-03. This amount has been reduced to Rs.50 crores for the year 2003-04 (rs.25 crores as
plan and Rs.25 crores as non-plan).
3.4       The Committee observes that with the introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards,
upgradation of automotive testing facilities is critically needed for further growth of automotive industry in the country. There is
also a need to look at other areas of product and process related research with a view to propelling India’s automotive industry
into a higher league and for surviving the import surge under WTO regime.  The required level of R&D  can be achieved only
by enhanced funding.  It is a fact that the Government is collecting automotive cess at the rate of 0.125%  per cent over and
above excise duty on vehicles. But since inception in 1984-85,  allocation of funds has been meager and much less than the
actual collection. Now  a comprehensive project on upgrading the testing infrastructure in the country is proposed to be
implemented at a cost of Rs.1500 crore. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the Government should enhance allocation
under cess to the extent of full amount collected. The Government should also allocate in two installments the entire unallocated

sum of Rs 347.38 crore. The Ministry should strive to attain the international level in R&D so that 100% indigenisation in
manufacturing of components takes place and import bill on auto components is reduced.
3.5       The Committee also notes that  at present the cess for  R&D is levied @ 1/8% i.e. 0.125% over  and above the excise
duty.  Department of Heavy Industry has, however, taken up the matter with the Ministry of Finance for enhancement in the rate
of levy of cess from 0.05% to 0.25%. The Committee strongly supports the view point of Department of Heavy Industry and
hopes Ministry of Finance would respond to the demand. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the progress made in
regard to the enhancement of rate of levy of cess from 0.05% to
0.25%. 
3.6       The Committee is of the view that while Government will no doubt provide funds for R&D activities within the given
availability of funds, at the same time there is an urgent need for the industry also to contribute towards R&D activities in auto
sector particularly in view of the fact that the entire auto sector is in the private sector. Hitherto, the contribution by the industry
for the R&D activities is negligible.

BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICAL LTD.
14.       Bharat Heavy Electricals ltd. (BHEL) was set up primarily to meet the needs of the power sector in the country. At

present, BHEL has 14 manufacturing divisions, 9 service centres and 4 Power sector regional centres in addition to a large
number of project sites spread all over India and abroad, enabling BHEL to serve the customers and the country promptly and
effectively. Besides. BHEL has a Corporate R&D complex at Hyderabad, HRD Institute at Delhi and Research Centre in all
manufacturing plants. .
14.1     BHEL manufactures over 180 products under 30 major product groups and meets the need of core sectors like power,
industry, transmission, transportation, defence, telecommunications, oil business, etc.Power is the core sector of B HEL and
comprises of thermal, nuclear, gas, diesel and  hydro business. BHEL built sets account for nearly 65% of the country's total
installed power generating capacity.
14.2     BHEL has made a major contribution in the areas of process industry, transportation, transmission, telecommunication,
non-conventional energy and other new products.  BHEL contributes major capital equipment and systems like captive power
plants, centrifugal compressors, drive turbines, pumps, heat exchangers, electric motors, valves, heavy castings and forgings,
etc. to the core industries viz. cement, metallurgical, mining, refineries, petro-chemicals, chemicals, etc. The Company has also
emerged as a major supplier of controls and instrumentation systems. In the transmission sector, besides producing high voltage
transformers and switchgear,  BHEL supplies equipment for high voltage direct current systems. The Company has also been
supplying oil-field equipment to ONGC and Oil India. Most of the trains in Indian Railways are equipped with BHEL's traction
control equipment. BHEL also manufactures AC/DC locos, battery powered road vehicles, OHE cars and motorized.
14.3     The Committee observes that power manufacture sector accounts for major business of BHEL(70%) apart from Industry
(20% ) and international market (10%) .  There is a great potential in power sector due to gap  between demand  and supply of
power.  But due to low investment , projects are not  coming up fast .  State electricity Board are major handicap in this regard.
14.4     The Committee therefore, recommends that  with the target of achieving 10,000 MW of additional capacity in power
generation by 2010 , there  is a need  to make huge  investments in the power sector .  Government of  India should  ensure that 
all possible steps  are taken  to see that  this sector does  not suffer due to resource  crunch Department of Heavy industry should
consider the matter regarding liquidation of outstanding dues of BHEL to be paid by SEBs afresh.  Committee hopes that  
Electricity   Bill will    be cleared by Parliament soon which will  improve the working of  SEBs and streamline their operations
which will be of help to BHEL also.  As regards the import of technology and operation of multinational companies
participating in bidding for large contracts in infrastructure building, suitable measures/precautions are needed to safeguard  the
Indian companies like BHEL and also reduce outflow  of capital from the country.  
14.5     Citing the example of China the Committee was apprised that whenever a technology is  brought in,  Chinese Govt.
stipulate that  over-seas company must associate a Chinese company in the process of manufacturing.  When a large  contract is

120th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/120threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:28:06]
awarded to over-seas non-Chinese company, China makes it a requirement that a part of that business  i.e.40  per cent must
come to  Chinese company.  Similarly, Malaysia has got ‘Bhumiputra policy’.   Bhumiputra Company,  which is registered in
Malaysia, will  have to be associated.  When technology is imported, local company must be associated.  China is doing it very
efficiently,   whereas,  India is  not doing it.  The technologies are brought in and  a local company is associated with the
technology and, gradually, indigenisation happens.
14.6     The Committee ,therefore recommends that when technologies are outsourced, Indian Government should make it
mandatory that  an Indian company is associated with the foreign partner in order to   absorb the technology  to the local needs.
The foreign firm  should have a tie-up with an Indian company. Multinational corporations are often bidding for large contracts
of infrastructure building etc. in the country. The Government should consider imposing conditions requiring involvement of at
least one Indian business entity.
14.7     The Committee was also apprised  that in order to create  capacity  for power generation BHEL must get order within
one-and-half years ahead  of the schedule.  If orders  are not placed  to BHEL beforehand, it will not be able to manufacture
necessary equipments for power generation in time. It was further stated that  18000 MW  capacity addition  are still to be
ordered.  If these are not ordered by September, 2003, then addition is not likely to  materialize.  It will then slip to the next 
Plan, . Only 50 per cent of  BHEL capacity  for  power infrastructure  as against the target of 30000 MW was achieved.  The 
Tenth  Plan has  a target of 40000 MW.
14.8     The Committee  therefore, recommends  that Department of Heavy Industries should ensure that orders for creating 
capacity  for power  generation  is     given  well in advance to BHEL, so that BHEL is able to achieve the target  in time.

15.2     The Committee came to know  that due to inadequate investments  in the traditional market segment of petroleum
refineries, the growth has not been upto the mark. In the diversified sector, especially, in the express highways, the Company is
yet to consolidate its business and build up the equipments as it has not been able to invest on equipment. This is considered

without any substantial  budgetary support from the Government. It hardly got Rs.2-3 crores two years ago. Primarily it had to
generate its own fund which went  into investment in construction machinery and as a result of that it had not been able to
repay the Government loan. The interest thereon   has been rising.
15.3    The Committee therefore, observes that there is a need for the financial restructuring of the company to clean its 
balance-sheet. It has  working capital problem. Whatever money it was able to generate, it has not been  able to put it in the
working capital for equipments. Therefore there was hardly any investment in equipment. The  deployment of most modern
equipment  replacing  the old conventional equipment is need of the hour as the method of construction has totally changed.
The award of package, has also changed from conventional to Lump Sum Turnkey Projects (LSTK)  package. So are  the fund
requirement for working capital and  equipment etc.  The turnover would  increase, provided it is able to invest more in
equipment etc.  The Company is not able  to raise  money  from the market because of its outstanding loan  If the loan amount
is converted into equity, no fund is required.  The interest  rate as high as is  18 percent.  If  the Company fails to   repay  the
loan, penal rate would be Rs.22.5 percent for  a loan that was taken almost 15 years ago.   The Committee  recommends that the
company’s Rs.11.00  crores  of loan  which has an  interest burden of Rs. 27 crores should be converted into equity . Since the

Recommendation
 
 1.9 Cost components of products produced by NMDC
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC management has introduced the muli-skilling concept to reduced the
fixed cost. The Committee also notes that various managerial controls measures are at work to reduce the cost of production.
The Committee desires that the Ministry of Steel, in its action Taken Note of the present Report, would furnish the detail as
to what extent the cost reduction measure entailed tangible result.
(PARA 10.4)
 Action Taken
 
The cost reduction measure undertaken by company is given below:
 
(a)
    fixing of standard cost at the beginning of the year for internal target production
(b)   comparison of actual cost with the standard cost monthly at project level
(c)    remedial measures to contain the cost at project level.
(d)   Monthly review of cost at Head Office by the management
 
Standard Cost per unit of iron ore / diamonds is prepared at the beginning of the year on the basis of production and
dispatch / sales targets finalized in the Corporate Plan meeting.  Project wise standard cost is projected considering the bench
marks in respect of each element of expenditure.  The bench marking is done considering the best of the physical parameters
achieved in the previous year, the average of previous five years or the standard set for the previous year, whichever reflects

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

efficiency, economy and effectiveness.  These physical parameters are regularly monitored by concerned departments viz
Production, Industrial Engineering and Finance  at the project as well as at Head Office.  The physical norms thus
established, for consumption such as ‘powder factor’ for explosives, ‘consumption per tonne of excavation’ for drill bits,
tyres & tubes, stores/spares , power etc., and the latest landed cost of the materials at the time of preparation of standard cost
are taken into account to project the expenditure for the target production quantity.  
 
The standard cost as estimated above are reviewed at HO by Directors and approved by the Chairman for
communicating the same to the units for monitoring the actual cost periodically.
 
There after, the actual cost of production is compared with the standard cost periodically at the project level.  The said
procedure of fixing standard costs is being followed consistently and wherever required, the same is being suitably modified
so that effective cost control can be made by the Corporation.
 
At the projects, during monthly review meetings of all HOD’s, the cost of production is discussed for minimizing the 
costs keeping in view the standard cost envisaged for that year.   At Head Office also, every month, the actual cost up to the
month is reviewed with previous year cost as well as standard cost and deviations are brought to the notice of the
management.   The actual cost of production vis-à-vis the standard cost, is also discussed and reviewed in the Annual / Mid-
Term Corporate Meetings.
 
            In addition, the units prepare cost sheets periodically covering all the cost centers and circulate to the respective
departments.   The same is reviewed in the project review meetings for taking remedial action wherever necessary.

Government has taken following steps to rationalize the procedure for renewal of mining lease:
A new rule 63A has been incorporated in the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 vide GSR21(E) dated 11
th
January,2002 which stipulate time limit of six months for Reconnaissance Permit, time limit of nine months for Prospecting
license and time limit of 12 months for Mining lease.
 
A new sub Rule 4B has been incorporated in rule 22 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 vide G.S.R. 21(E) dated
11th January,2002 which provides a time limit of 90 days for approval of mining plans submitted by prospective applicants.
 
Rule 22 (4A of Mineral concession Rule 1960 ) has been amended for allowing Director or Additional Director or
Joint Director (Mining & Geology) of a State, with essential educational qualifications & professional experience as
prescribed, to approve the mining plan irrespective of the pay scale.
 
The recent procedural simplification provided that in case of renewal of mining lease, the entrepreneur could
approach Central Government directly for necessary clearance and get a time bound decision,  if  State Government did not
take a decision on the application in prescribed time.

3.3 Major customers of NMDC in domestic and foreign market and need of autonomy for NMDC in export promotion i.e.
direct export by NMDC
 
            The Committee notes that NMDC sells 55% of its production for the domestic market while 45% is being sold out to
international market. The Committee wonders that even in the age of liberalization and globalization the Government
continues with policy of allowing the service of canalizing agency. De-canalization should have followed theliberalization
policy. While de-canalisation applies with one of PSUs under the Ministry of steel i.e. Metal Scrap Trade Corporation
Limited (MSTC) and the same principle has not been applied in the case of NMDC. As per the existing system, Iron-Ore is
to be exported through canalizing agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to Iron ore with 65% Fe content and above
whereas NMDC has got more quantity of Iron Ore lying in its pit head with less than fifty  five percent Iron content for
which international market is available but the same is not explored by NMDC. Therefore, the Committee feels that, it
would be in the fitness of things that NMDC is given complete autonomy in the best-interest of the Company. The
Committee feels NMDC be allowed to direct export to the countries other than the purchaser from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pak
and South Korea, NMDC has already exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 Lakh tones in 1999-2000, 9.65 Lakh tones
in 2000-01, and thus experience so gained, would proved handy to NMDC in direct export of Iron-ore. 
(PARA 21.11.4)
 
    Government is aware of the need for de-canalization of iron-ore. However, in view of the Long Term Agreement for
export of iron ore by MMTC, Govt. has decided that the existing arrangement for export of high quality iron –ore (with Fe
content of 645 and above) through MMTC may continue.
 
            After government intervention, an agreement was reached as per which NMDC has been entrusted with more
responsibility for all operational matters, including rail handling up-to loading into the ship. MMTC also agreed to reduce
the service charge from 5-6% of FOB to 3% on FOB value. This agreement has given NMDC a large role in export
operations.
 
             For the year 2002-03, NMDC has now been permitted to export 30  LMT (15 LMT from Bailadila and 15 LMT
from Donimalai). NMDC has also been granted export license for the following quantities:
 
Year Bailadila Donimalai Total
2003-04 17 LMT 18LMT 35 LMT
2004-05 17LMT 23LMT 40 LMT
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee is of the view that NMDC should be allowed to direct export to the countries rather than through
MMTC to the order of substantial quantity.  Time frame for how long export of iron ore through MMTC would continue has
not been indicated.  The Committee feels that functional autonomy given to NMDC in regard to direct export would enhance
the operational efficiency of the company in direct marketing.
